docs.title: ETLRelay
docs.text:
ETLRelay is an open-source Python framework for composing lightweight, batch-oriented extract, transform, and load (ETL) pipelines.

Its core execution model is:

Source → Processor(s) → Sink

A source produces batches, processors transform them, and a sink consumes the processed output. File workflows keep storage access independent of format-specific reading and writing.

docs.title: v1.0.0 — Stable initial release
docs.text:
This documentation describes ETLRelay v1.0.0 and its supported public contract. Install etlrelay==1.0.0. The release retains the verified v0.9.0 Python APIs, local CSV/Parquet and SQLite workflows, processors, YAML schema version 1, and CLI behavior. No code or configuration migration is required from v0.9.0.

Start with Getting Started, the compatibility policy, and release notes. For releases before v0.9.0, use the migration guide.

docs.title: Current capabilities
docs.text:
ETLRelay includes:

  • Arrow-backed Batch data and synchronous pipeline execution.
  • The etlrelay CLI with run, validate, version, and help commands.
  • Local filesystem access with resolved-path containment validation.
  • CSV and Parquet reading and writing.
  • Column selection, column renaming, and row filtering processors.
  • SQLAlchemy-backed SqlSource and append-only SqlSink.
  • YAML configuration schema version 1 with explicit component validation.
  • ComponentCatalog and PipelineBuilder for configuration-built pipelines.
  • Resource lifecycle management and documented error propagation.
  • Unit, integration, functional, and installed-distribution tests.

SQLite is the reference SQL integration-test backend. Other SQLAlchemy dialects require appropriate drivers and application-level verification.

ETLRelay supports CPython 3.12, 3.13, and 3.14. The complete test suite runs on Python 3.12, with installed wheel/source-distribution compatibility checks across the declared Python/platform matrix. See the packaging verification record for verification evidence.

See the v1.0.0 readiness record for verification evidence and release gates.

docs.title: Scope and limitations
docs.text:
YAML schema version 1 supports file and SQL sources/sinks, local CSV/Parquet workflows, and the built-in select_columns, rename_columns, and filter_rows processors.

The configuration model uses explicit registrations rather than arbitrary dynamic imports or a general-purpose plugin system.

The validate command parses and validates configuration without constructing runtime components, resolving SQL environment variables, or executing the pipeline. Builder preflight occurs during run; neither validation nor preflight guarantees runtime data compatibility, filesystem availability, or database connectivity.

File writes are non-atomic, and SQL sink transactions operate per nonempty batch. ETLRelay does not automatically retry failed operations or roll back earlier persisted output.

S3, HDFS, and other remote-storage integrations remain outside the planned v1.0.0 scope.

Public interfaces follow the compatibility policy. Users remain responsible for evaluating deployment security and operational requirements.

docs.title: API Reference
docs.text:
This reference documents ETLRelay's public Python interfaces and implementations using their source-code docstrings.

The v0.9.0 API review retains the synchronous pipeline model and configuration schema version 1. Tabular stream protocols are now named TabularReader and TabularWriter; update imports of the former class names. See the API review for decisions and compatibility notes.

Important runtime behaviors include:

  • Local filesystem path containment and explicit stream ownership.
  • Lazy batch processing and deterministic cleanup of closeable pipeline iterators.
  • Output-schema validation, including zero-row batches.
  • SQLAlchemy connection and result cleanup.
  • Per-batch SQL transactions and append-only persistence.
  • Configuration validation and SQL environment-variable preflight.
  • Exception propagation and controlled operational logging.

The Python API generally preserves underlying runtime exceptions. The CLI provides separate error-reporting and exit-code conventions, documented in the CLI Reference.

Configuration schema version 1 remains supported and is independent of the ETLRelay package version.

The documented public interfaces and import paths are stable from v1.0.0. See the compatibility policy for guarantees, exclusions, and release/deprecation rules.

Consult the YAML Configuration, Security, Logging, and Architecture documentation for detailed usage contracts and limitations.

The catalog registers CSV and Parquet readers and writers, local filesystem storage, file and SQL sources and sinks, and the select_columns, rename_columns, and filter_rows processors. It also assembles the dispatchers and root configuration validator.

A single set of registries is shared between the corresponding validators and factories, and the same SQL engine factory is supplied to both SQL component factories.

docs.title: etlrelay.config.pipeline_builder.PipelineBuilder
docs.text:
Build runtime pipelines from validated configuration mappings.

The builder resolves source, processor, and sink registrations before invoking component factories. SQL environment references are preflighted before component construction to prevent missing or empty environment variables from causing partial pipeline construction.

getenv provides a lightweight environment lookup for isolated builder use and tests. In the default application composition, the shared SqlEngineFactory should be supplied so successful preflight makes resolved connection URLs available to SQL component factories.

The builder does not execute the pipeline it constructs. When a shared SQL engine factory is supplied, the caller is responsible for closing the builder after pipeline execution to release the factory's resources.

docs.text:
Resolve SQL connection URLs and manage SQLAlchemy engine lifecycles.

Environment-variable references must pass preflight before engines can be created. Successful preflight stores resolved connection URLs without creating engines. Engines are created on demand and cached by environment variable name.

The factory owns the engines it creates and disposes of them when close() is called. Closing also discards resolved connection URLs. Environment lookup and engine creation can be injected for testing.

docs.title: preflight(references)
docs.text:
Resolve and validate all referenced connection environment variables.

The mapping associates configuration paths with environment-variable names. Each unique variable is read once, and missing or empty values are aggregated into a single error. No engines are created during preflight.

A successful preflight replaces any previous resolved URL set. A failed preflight leaves resolved URLs unavailable for engine creation. Preflight cannot be repeated while the factory has active engines.

docs.title: etlrelay.pipeline.pipeline.Pipeline
docs.text:
Coordinate batch processing between a source, processors, and a sink.

The pipeline obtains batches from a source, applies each configured processor in sequence, validates the resulting output schemas, and passes compatible batches to the sink.

The first processed output batch establishes the expected schema for the run. Subsequent output batches must have matching field names, field order, Arrow types, and nullability. Schema metadata differences are ignored. Zero-row batches participate in schema validation.

Processing is lazy and does not buffer all batches before writing. If a later batch has an incompatible schema, a ValueError is raised before that batch is yielded to the sink. Batches successfully written before a later failure are not rolled back.

Exceptions from the source, processors, or sink otherwise propagate to the caller.

Pipeline owns the consumption lifecycle of the source iterator for the duration of run(). When execution terminates, it attempts to close both the processing iterator and the underlying source iterator when they provide callable close() methods.

This cleanup occurs after successful execution, early sink termination, or failures during source iteration, processing, or sink execution.

Execution exceptions take precedence over iterator cleanup failures. Secondary cleanup failures are logged without their exception messages. If execution otherwise succeeds but cleanup fails, the first cleanup exception propagates.

Pipeline does not own or dispose the underlying storage backends, database engines, or component instances.

docs.text:
Append batches to the target SQL table.

Each non-empty batch is inserted within its own transaction. Empty batches are skipped without opening a transaction. Batch columns are validated against the target table before insertion.

Previously committed batches remain committed if a later batch fails. A failure during a batch write rolls back that batch's transaction and propagates the exception to the caller.

required

Note

SqlSink borrows the supplied SQLAlchemy Engine and does not dispose it.

Each nonempty batch is written in a separate transaction. A transaction commits only after its context manager exits successfully. Failed transactions are rolled back by SQLAlchemy, while previously committed batches remain committed.

Zero-row batches are skipped before reflection, column validation, or transaction creation.

Batch columns must be unique and exist in the destination table. Omitted destination columns are permitted when supported by database defaults, nullability, or other database rules.

SqlSink does not create tables, migrate schemas, upsert rows, or provide a transaction spanning multiple batches.

docs.title: Command-Line Interface Reference
docs.text:
This reference describes ETLRelay v1.0.0. See Getting Started for a complete installation and pipeline example.

ETLRelay provides a command-line interface (CLI) for validating and executing supported YAML pipeline configurations. Install ETLRelay into the Python environment where you intend to run it, then invoke the etlrelay command from a terminal.

python -m pip install etlrelay==1.0.0
etlrelay --help
etlrelay version

The package supports CPython 3.12–3.14 (>=3.12,<3.15). See Getting Started for installation and a complete local CSV example, and YAML Configuration for the supported schema and component properties.

docs.title: General usage
docs.text:
etlrelay [OPTIONS] COMMAND [ARGS]...

-h and --help display help. Run etlrelay --help for the command list or append --help to a command to inspect its arguments and options. Running etlrelay without a command also displays root help.

docs.title: etlrelay run PIPELINE
docs.text:
Load, validate, build, and execute the pipeline defined in the YAML file at PIPELINE.

etlrelay run pipeline.yaml

The configuration must describe supported source, processor, and sink components. Relative filesystem paths should be configured deliberately; use the same working directory assumed by the configuration's local storage base_path.

On success, the command prints a confirmation to standard output, for example:

Pipeline completed: pipeline.yaml

A configuration loading or validation failure exits with code 3. An unexpected internal or pipeline-construction error exits with code 1. A source, processor, sink, or runtime-resource-cleanup failure exits with code 4.

docs.title: etlrelay validate PIPELINE
docs.text:
Parse and validate a YAML pipeline configuration without building or executing the pipeline.

etlrelay validate pipeline.yaml

On success, the command prints a confirmation to standard output:

Pipeline configuration is valid: pipeline.yaml

Validation checks configuration syntax and the supported schema. It does not prove that an input file exists, that runtime data contains every referenced column, that a database connection will succeed, or that the output destination is writable. Those conditions may only become apparent when the pipeline is built or run.

Configuration, YAML parsing, file-access, and validation failures exit with code 3. Unexpected internal failures exit with code 1.

docs.title: etlrelay version
docs.text:
Print the installed package version from distribution metadata.

etlrelay version

Example output:

etlrelay 1.0.0

If the installed package version cannot be determined from metadata, the command exits with code 1 and writes a diagnostic to standard error.

docs.title: etlrelay help [COMMAND]
docs.text:
Display general help or help for a named command.

etlrelay help
etlrelay help run
etlrelay help validate

An unknown help target is a usage error and exits with code 2. The normal --help option is also supported, for example etlrelay run --help.

docs.title: Exit codes
docs.text:
The CLI uses the following process exit codes:

Code Meaning Typical examples 0 Success Help/version displayed; validation passes; pipeline completes 1 Unexpected internal error Unexpected configuration-loading or pipeline-construction failure; package version metadata unavailable 2 Command usage error Missing required argument, invalid invocation, or unknown command supplied to etlrelay help 3 Configuration or build failure Malformed YAML, invalid configuration, inaccessible configuration file, or PipelineBuildError 4 Runtime execution or cleanup failure Source read fails, a processor fails, a sink write fails, or builder cleanup fails

Use the exit code for automation rather than parsing the diagnostic text.

docs.title: Standard output and standard error
docs.text:
• Standard output (stdout) contains help, version information, and successful command confirmations.
  • Standard error (stderr) contains usage, configuration, validation, execution, and unexpected-error diagnostics.
  • Successful commands return exit code 0; failures return the code associated with the failure category above.
  • Runtime execution diagnostics include the exception type and a general troubleshooting hint, but omit the underlying runtime exception message and traceback.
  • Configuration-validator and pipeline-builder diagnostics may include their own error details to identify the invalid configuration. Do not place credentials or other secrets in YAML values or error messages; reference SQL connection URLs through environment-variable names as described in YAML Configuration.

The CLI's error presentation is intended to be useful without printing runtime payloads. It is not a substitute for controlling access to process environments, configuration files, or application logs.

docs.title: Example: local CSV pipeline
docs.text:
Create input.csv in a working directory:

id,amount,state
1,10,ready
2,-2,skip
3,5,ready

Create pipeline.yaml in the same directory:

version: 1

source:
  type: file
  path: input.csv
  format: csv
  storage:
    type: local
    base_path: .

processors:
  - type: select_columns
    columns: [id, amount]
  - type: filter_rows
    column: amount
    operator: ">"
    value: 0
  - type: rename_columns
    mapping:
      id: record_id

sink:
  type: file
  path: output.csv
  format: csv
  storage:
    type: local
    base_path: .

From that working directory, validate and run the pipeline:

etlrelay validate pipeline.yaml
etlrelay run pipeline.yaml

The resulting output.csv contains the positive-amount rows with id renamed to record_id. The configured processor list runs in order. The schema and available component properties are documented in YAML Configuration.

docs.title: Automation notes
docs.text:
• Use etlrelay validate pipeline.yaml before scheduling or invoking etlrelay run pipeline.yaml, but remember that validation cannot guarantee runtime resources will be available.
  • Check the documented process exit code to decide whether an automated job succeeded.
  • Keep credentials out of YAML configuration and diagnostic text. Use environment-variable references for SQL connection URLs.
  • The CLI is synchronous. It does not provide scheduling, retries, background jobs, or a daemon.

docs.title: YAML document-shape failures
docs.text:
An empty document, a non-mapping root, or a root with non-string keys is a configuration failure. Both validate and run return exit code 3 and report the required document shape without echoing document contents.

validate does not construct runtime components or resolve SQL connection environment variables. SQL environment preflight occurs during run when PipelineBuilder constructs the pipeline.

docs.title: Compatibility and Versioning Policy
docs.text: This policy applies from ETLRelay v1.0.0. The supported product and environment matrix are defined in the scope and support policy. The API reference, configuration reference, and CLI reference define the behavior covered by this policy.

docs.title: Stable public contract
docs.text:
Surface Compatibility commitment Python API Documented public import paths, names, constructors, arguments, protocol signatures, return values, and documented exception types/conditions remain compatible within a major release. Data and execution Documented Batch schema/empty-data semantics, processor predicates and null handling, ordering, exception propagation, ownership, cleanup, overwrite behavior, and transaction boundaries remain compatible. YAML schema version 1 Existing valid configurations keep their meaning and remain usable within ETLRelay 1.x. Schema version and package version are independent. CLI Documented commands, arguments/options, exit codes, and explicitly specified output contracts remain compatible within a major release. Supported environments Removing a declared Python/platform combination or tested database from support is a breaking change. New verified combinations may be added compatibly.

Use the responsibility-level convenience packages documented in the API reference, such as etlrelay.core, etlrelay.readers, and etlrelay.pipeline. Public classes and functions explicitly documented through their implementation modules are also covered, including configuration services and registrations. These import paths remain supported even if internal organization changes. The root etlrelay package does not provide an umbrella re-export API.

TabularReader and TabularWriter are the public tabular protocols. KeyValueReader reads a mapping-shaped document and remains separate from row records. The former Reader/Writer class names were removed in v0.9.0 and are not restored by v1.0.0. See the migration guide when upgrading from earlier releases. No code or YAML migration is needed from v0.9.0 to v1.0.0.

docs.title: Release rules
docs.text:
ETLRelay follows Semantic Versioning:

  • Patch (1.0.1): Compatible correctness, security, documentation, packaging, or maintenance fixes. Correcting behavior to match the documented contract may change the outcome of previously invalid or defective usage.
  • Minor (1.1.0): Backward-compatible additions. Existing supported calls, configurations, and workflows retain their documented behavior. New optional configuration fields may be accepted, but existing schema version 1 settings must preserve their meaning.
  • Major (2.0.0): Incompatible changes to the supported contract, including removal/renaming of public imports, incompatible argument/return or failure semantics, changed persistence guarantees, or rejection/reinterpretation of previously valid configuration. A new schema version does not justify breaking existing version 1 support within ETLRelay 1.x.

A security fix follows the same compatibility classification. If a required fix cannot preserve the supported contract, document the impact and migration and publish an appropriate major release rather than silently weakening this policy.

Published package files and tagged source are not replaced. Corrections use a new release and updated release notes. Historical documentation stays pinned to its release; current documentation and repository examples use the target version rather than moving branches or documentation aliases.

docs.title: Deprecation and migration
docs.text:
Introduce public deprecations in a minor release, document the replacement and migration, and retain the deprecated contract throughout the remainder of that major line. Use a DeprecationWarning for Python APIs where practical. Remove supported deprecated behavior only in a subsequent major release, after at least one minor release has carried the notice. No fixed calendar support period is promised.

Document breaking changes and required migration in the changelog, release notes, and relevant references. Pre-1.0 migration notes remain historical guidance.

docs.title: Boundaries and exclusions
docs.text:
The compatibility promise does not turn every importable object or upstream behavior into ETLRelay's public API. It excludes:

  • Private names and modules (leading _), undocumented helpers/attributes, internal call order, and internal registry/cache representations.
  • Exact wording, formatting, timestamps, ordering, or volume of help text, human-readable errors, and operational logs, except output explicitly specified as a CLI contract. Use documented exit codes for command failure handling.
  • Exact messages/types of arbitrary third-party exceptions where ETLRelay only promises propagation; documented ETLRelay exception contracts remain covered.
  • Byte-for-byte serialized output, performance thresholds, or external library internals beyond ETLRelay's documented data/schema and format behavior.
  • Untested database dialects, undeclared Python/platform combinations, unsupported usage, and deferred features listed in the scope policy.

Dependency constraints are declared in package metadata and verified in CI. Dependency upgrades require regression and artifact checks appropriate to their impact; they do not automatically expand ETLRelay's supported environments or public functionality. The lockfile records release verification inputs rather than promising every transitive version will remain fixed throughout 1.x.

The stable contract includes the existing limitations: local writes can truncate files and leave partial output; SQL output appends to existing tables with one transaction per nonempty batch; earlier committed output survives later failures. Path containment is not a sandbox, and controlled diagnostics do not guarantee sanitization of arbitrary third-party logs. See Security.

docs.title: Release acceptance
docs.text: Maintainer verification establishes readiness using the existing test, quality, artifact, documentation, dependency, and support-matrix checks. External beta participation, a minimum user count, and an RC cycle are optional. They are not acceptance requirements for v1.0.0. New features and broader adoption work are considered through a separate post-v1.0 roadmap.

docs.title: Core Concepts
docs.text:
ETLRelay composes batch-oriented ETL pipelines from a source, an ordered sequence of processors, and a sink.

Source → Processor(s) → Sink

A source produces batches, processors transform them, and a sink consumes the processed output. For file workflows, ETLRelay separates storage access from format-specific reading and writing.

docs.title: Batch
docs.text:
A Batch wraps a pyarrow.Table and provides the common tabular data representation used throughout ETLRelay.

The table retains its values and Arrow schema, including field names, field order, data types, and nullability. A processor may change the schema as part of a transformation; otherwise, the schema is preserved.

A batch containing zero rows is still a valid batch. Its schema remains available even when it contains no data rows.

docs.title: Source, Processor, and Sink
docs.text:
A Source implements read() and produces an iterable of batches.

A Processor implements:

process(batch: Batch) -> Batch

Processors operate on individual batches. The pipeline applies them in their configured order, passing each processor's output to the next processor. ETLRelay includes processors for selecting columns, renaming columns, and filtering rows. Applications can also provide implementations that satisfy the processor contract.

A Sink consumes an iterable of processed batches. A file sink composes a storage implementation with a writer to write batches to a configured destination.

docs.title: Storage and File Formats
docs.text:
Storage provides binary streams; readers and writers handle file formats.

FileSource → FileSystem → BinaryIO → TabularReader → Batch

Batch iterable → TabularWriter → BinaryIO → FileSystem → Destination

FileSource composes a filesystem with a reader. FileSink composes a filesystem with a writer. This separates resource access from format-specific parsing and serialization.

The built-in local storage and tabular formats are LocalFileSystem, CSV, and Parquet. Select the reader and writer explicitly when composing FileSource and FileSink; the file extension does not select a format automatically.

docs.title: CSV and Parquet Behavior
docs.text:
Behavior CSV Parquet Representation Text; no embedded Arrow schema Columnar binary format with schema and type information Reading types PyArrow infers types from text; exact schema round trips are not guaranteed Preserves supported schema/type information represented in the file Multiple batches Serializes batches in order; a CSV stream has one header written by the first batch Serializes batches in order into one Parquet file Zero-row batch with schema Can write a header-only CSV Writes a valid schema-bearing zero-row Parquet file; the reader yields an empty batch with the schema Empty batch iterable Writes no bytes Raises WriterError because no schema is available to initialize the file Stream requirements Binary stream TabularReader requires a seekable binary stream; writer requires a writable binary stream supported by PyArrow

A zero-row batch and an empty batch iterable are different: the former still carries an Arrow schema; the latter carries no batch from which a schema can be obtained. ParquetWriter uses the first batch's schema and requires following batches to have the same schema. ETLRelay does not merge incompatible schemas or automatically cast batches.

The component that opens a stream retains responsibility for its lifecycle; readers and writers must not close caller-owned streams.

docs.title: Declarative Configuration
docs.text:
ETLRelay supports schema-versioned YAML configuration as an alternative to direct Python composition. The supported configuration surface is deliberately fixed: file and SQL sources/sinks, local storage, CSV/Parquet file formats, and the built-in column-selection, renaming, and row-filtering processors.

The workflow is:

YAML file
   ↓
ConfigLoader + KeyValueReader/YamlReader
   ↓
ConfigValidator
   ↓
Validated mapping
   ↓
PipelineBuilder + shared ComponentCatalog
   ↓
Pipeline
   ↓
Pipeline.run()

A mapping-shaped configuration document is not a tabular Batch stream. KeyValueReader is a separate protocol from the current tabular TabularReader protocol. YamlReader handles YAML syntax and document shape; ConfigValidator handles ETLRelay's schema; PipelineBuilder resolves explicit registrations and constructs runtime components. Neither loading nor schema validation builds or executes a pipeline.

Configuration schema version 1 requires exactly version, source, processors, and sink. Unknown fields and unsupported component types are rejected. SQL source/sink connection URLs are referenced by environment-variable name, then checked during builder preflight before component factories and source/sink I/O begin. See YAML Configuration for properties, combinations, errors, and examples.

docs.title: Pipeline Execution
docs.text:
Pipeline coordinates the source, processors, and sink. Execution is synchronous, and batches are processed sequentially in source order.

The pipeline does not buffer all source batches before writing. Processed batches are yielded incrementally to the sink.

docs.title: Output Schema Compatibility
docs.text:
The first processed output batch establishes the expected schema for a pipeline run. Every subsequent processed output batch must have a compatible schema.

Compatibility requires matching:

  • Field names
  • Field order
  • Arrow field types
  • Field nullability

Schema metadata differences are ignored when checking compatibility. Schema validation takes place after all configured processors have run. This allows processors to normalize inputs with different schemas into compatible output schemas.

If a processed batch has an incompatible schema, the pipeline raises ValueError before yielding that batch to the sink. The pipeline does not automatically merge schemas, cast values, or reconcile incompatible outputs. Zero-row batches participate in schema validation just like non-empty batches.

docs.title: Empty Sources and Zero-Row Batches
docs.text:
An empty source iterable and a zero-row batch represent different conditions.

  • Zero-row batch: The source produces a Batch containing a zero-row Arrow table. The batch passes through the configured processors, participates in schema validation, and is delivered to the sink if processing succeeds.
  • Empty source iterable: The source produces no batches. No processors are called, and the sink is not invoked.

The presence of a batch, rather than its row count, determines whether the pipeline has data to process.

docs.title: Exceptions and Partial Writes
docs.text:
Exceptions raised while reading from a source, iterating over its batches, processing a batch, validating its output schema, or writing to a sink propagate to the caller. ETLRelay does not wrap these errors in a separate pipeline exception hierarchy.

If a later batch fails, batches successfully written before the failure are not automatically rolled back. The pipeline does not provide transactional execution across multiple batches.

docs.title: Current Scope
docs.text:
ETLRelay provides synchronous, batch-oriented execution with local CSV/Parquet I/O, SQLAlchemy-backed SQL sources/sinks, a small set of built-in processors, and YAML-driven construction. SQLite is the reference SQL integration-test backend; other SQLAlchemy dialects require appropriate drivers and independent verification. SQL sink tables must already exist and be compatible with the output columns.

S3, HDFS, and other remote-storage backends remain outside the planned v1.0.0 scope. Scheduling, distributed execution, parallel processing, automatic retries, generic plugins, and automatic schema reconciliation are not provided by the current implementation. Additional capabilities should be introduced only when concrete requirements justify them.

docs.title: YAML Configuration
docs.text:
ETLRelay supports declarative pipelines using versioned YAML configuration. Schema version 1 defines a closed set of supported sources, processors, sinks, storage backends, and file formats.

Configuration validation checks the documented schema and component properties. Pipeline construction performs additional component-registration resolution and SQL connection-reference preflight before invoking component factories.

These checks detect supported configuration errors before execution, but they do not guarantee successful filesystem access, database operations, data processing, or output persistence.

Configuration schema version 1 is independent of the ETLRelay package version and remains unchanged for v0.9.0.

Use this page as the canonical reference for the schema. Getting Started demonstrates how to load, build, and execute a configuration; the configuration architecture pages explain the internal boundaries.

docs.title: Configuration lifecycle
docs.text:
Configuration loading, schema validation, component construction, and pipeline execution are separate stages:

  1. ConfigLoader opens and parses the configuration document through FileSystem and KeyValueReader. YamlReader is the built-in configuration reader.
  2. ConfigValidator checks schema version 1, required properties, component types, and component-specific configuration rules.
  3. PipelineBuilder resolves the configured component registrations and preflights SQL connection environment-variable references.
  4. After registration resolution and SQL preflight succeed, the builder invokes component factories and returns a Pipeline.
  5. The caller executes the pipeline and closes the builder afterward to release SQL engines owned by the shared factory.

The CLI exposes this workflow through etlrelay validate and etlrelay run, with distinct validation/construction and execution error reporting.

docs.title: Preflight guarantees
docs.text:
The supported validation and preflight checks establish that:

  • The YAML document satisfies the required parsing and root-shape rules.
  • The configuration uses schema version 1.
  • Required configuration properties are present and have supported types.
  • Unsupported properties and component types are rejected.
  • Configured components resolve through explicit registrations.
  • SQL connection_url_env values are valid environment-variable names.
  • Referenced SQL connection environment variables are present and nonempty during builder preflight.
  • Component factories are not invoked if registration resolution or required SQL environment preflight fails.

Schema validation does not execute source queries, process records, write pipeline output, or verify the compatibility of actual data with the configured processors and destinations.

docs.title: Preflight limitations
docs.text:
Successful configuration validation does not establish that:

  • Input files exist, are accessible, or contain valid data.
  • Output paths are writable or have sufficient available storage.
  • SQL connection URLs represent reachable databases.
  • Database credentials have the necessary permissions.
  • SQL queries are valid, authorized, or guaranteed to succeed.
  • Destination tables exist or accept the processed data.
  • Processors will accept every batch encountered during execution.
  • Different batches will have compatible Arrow schemas.
  • Execution will be atomic or recover automatically from failures.

The configuration document itself must be read during validation. Pipeline construction may allocate resources for configured components.

etlrelay validate checks the configured pipeline without executing its data-processing run. It also does not construct runtime components or resolve SQL environment variables; those steps belong to run. It is not a comprehensive runtime-readiness or security assessment.

docs.title: Root schema
docs.text:
Every schema-v1 document must contain exactly these top-level properties:

Property Required Type Contract version Yes integer Must be the integer 1; YAML Boolean true is not accepted as version 1. source Yes mapping One supported source definition. processors Yes list Ordered processor definitions. An empty list is valid and passes batches through unchanged. sink Yes mapping One supported sink definition.

Unknown top-level properties are rejected. Component definitions also have closed property sets, so misspelled or unsupported fields are rejected rather than ignored. Duplicate YAML mapping keys are rejected, including duplicates after YAML merge-key flattening.

The schema version is independent of the ETLRelay package version. Version 1 has no implicit fallback or migration. Incompatible configuration-structure changes require a new schema version; existing version-1 property meanings must remain stable.

docs.title: Supported component/property matrix
docs.text:
Area type / name Properties beyond type Notes Source file path, format, storage Format must support reading. Source sql connection_url_env, query; optional parameters Uses a preflighted connection URL from the named environment variable. Sink file path, format, storage Format must support writing. Sink sql connection_url_env, table_name; optional schema Appends to an existing table. Processor select_columns columns Ordered list of unique string column names. Processor rename_columns mapping Mapping of string source names to string target names. Processor filter_rows column, operator, value Predicate value must be a string, integer, float, or Boolean. Storage local Optional base_path Defaults to .. File input format csv, parquet source.format Each registered format must support reading. File output format csv, parquet sink.format Each registered format must support writing.

No other source, sink, processor, storage backend, or file format is supported by schema version 1.

docs.title: File source and sink
docs.text:
A file source and file sink use the same required property names:

Property Required Type Meaning type Yes string: file Selects the file source or sink. path Yes non-empty string Input or output path. format Yes string: csv or parquet Explicitly selects a registered reader or writer. Format is not inferred from the filename extension. storage Yes mapping Storage component configuration. storage.type Yes string: local Selects LocalFileSystem. storage.base_path No non-empty string Permitted base directory; defaults to ..

Relative base_path values are resolved from the process working directory; relative path values are resolved under that base directory. Absolute paths are accepted only if they remain within the configured base. PathValidator enforces path containment; it is not a complete OS-level sandbox.

The base directory and any needed parent directories must already exist. Local output creates a new file if necessary and truncates an existing output file; it does not create missing parent directories.

Source and sink formats are selected independently, so all four file-to-file combinations are supported: CSV→CSV, CSV→Parquet, Parquet→CSV, and Parquet→Parquet.

docs.title: SQL source
docs.text:
Property Required Type Meaning type Yes string: sql Selects SqlSource. connection_url_env Yes valid environment-variable identifier Name of an environment variable containing a SQLAlchemy connection URL; literal URLs are not accepted in this field. query Yes non-empty string Caller-authored SQL query. Use named bind parameters for query values. parameters No mapping Named bind-parameter values. Keys must be strings; values may be strings, integers, floats, Booleans, or null.

Nested mappings and sequences are not supported as query-parameter values. Bound parameters are for values, not identifiers such as table or column names. Configuration validation does not parse SQL or enforce database authorization policy.

Example:

source:
  type: sql
  connection_url_env: ETLRELAY_SOURCE_DATABASE_URL
  query: "SELECT id, amount, state FROM source_records WHERE state = :state ORDER BY id"
  parameters:
    state: ready

docs.title: SQL sink
docs.text:
Property Required Type Meaning type Yes string: sql Selects SqlSink. connection_url_env Yes valid environment-variable identifier Name of an environment variable containing a SQLAlchemy connection URL; literal URLs are not accepted in this field. table_name Yes non-empty string Existing destination table to append rows to. schema No non-empty string Optional database schema name.

The destination table must already exist and accept the processed batch columns. The sink does not create, truncate, replace, or migrate tables. Each non-empty batch is written in its own transaction; a later failure does not roll back earlier committed batches. SQLite is the reference integration-test backend. Other SQLAlchemy dialects require their relevant drivers and independent verification.

SQL source and sink components can use the same environment-variable name or different names.

The configuration validator rejects connection_url_env values that do not have valid environment-variable identifier syntax. It does not interpret arbitrary strings or literal SQLAlchemy connection URLs as environment-variable references.

PipelineBuilder checks that each required variable resolves to a nonempty value before invoking component factories. It does not validate the contents of the resolved URL, establish a database connection as part of preflight, or verify database authorization.

Connection values must be supplied securely by the application's execution environment.

docs.title: Processor definitions
docs.text: The processors property is an ordered list. Processor n receives the output of processor n-1. An empty list is valid; omitting the property is invalid.

docs.title: select_columns
docs.text:
Property Required Type Contract type Yes string: select_columns Processor discriminator. columns Yes list of strings Names must be unique. The list determines output column order.

Column existence and ambiguity depend on the data schema and can fail during execution. An empty column list is accepted; it produces a zero-column Arrow table, which some output formats or databases cannot serialize. Use a nonempty selection for portable file/SQL output.

docs.title: rename_columns
docs.text:
Property Required Type Contract type Yes string: rename_columns Processor discriminator. mapping Yes mapping of string to string Source column name to desired column name.

The validator checks that the mapping and its keys/values have the required types. Whether source columns exist and whether final column names conflict is checked against the batch schema during processing.

docs.title: filter_rows
docs.text:
Property Required Type Contract type Yes string: filter_rows Processor discriminator. column Yes non-empty string Column to compare. operator Yes string One of ==, !=, <, <=, >, >=. value Yes string, integer, float, or Boolean null, mappings, and sequences are not accepted.

Column existence and comparison compatibility depend on the input data and may therefore fail at execution time. The validator does not inspect file contents or execute the processor.

docs.title: Supported source/sink combinations
docs.text:
The configured source and sink are independently selected from the supported formats and component types. This produces nine format/component combinations:

Source Sink Status and constraints CSV file CSV file Supported. CSV file Parquet file Supported. Parquet file CSV file Supported. Parquet file Parquet file Supported. CSV file SQL Supported. SQL target table must exist and accept the output columns. Parquet file SQL Supported. SQL target table must exist and accept the output columns. SQL CSV file Supported. Output path/base directory must be permitted and available. SQL Parquet file Supported. Output path/base directory must be permitted and available. SQL SQL Supported. Target table must exist and accept the output columns; source and sink may use same or separate connection variables.

These are supported combinations, not a guarantee that arbitrary queries, schemas, paths, values, or destination tables will work. Runtime checks and external system errors still apply.

docs.title: Operational semantics
docs.text: The configuration schema determines which components can be constructed. Runtime behavior follows the contracts of Pipeline and the selected source, processor, sink, and format implementations.

docs.title: Empty sources and zero-row batches
docs.text:
A source that produces no batches causes the pipeline to finish without invoking its sink.

A zero-row batch is different: it passes through the configured processors and participates in pipeline output-schema validation. If processing succeeds, it is delivered to the sink.

The concrete sink or writer determines how such a batch is persisted.

  • CsvWriter can write a CSV header for a schema-bearing zero-row batch.
  • ParquetWriter can write a valid zero-row Parquet file. A directly supplied empty iterable raises WriterError because no output schema can be established.
  • SqlSink skips zero-row batches before opening a transaction or validating destination columns.

docs.title: Output schema compatibility
docs.text:
The first processed batch establishes the expected pipeline output schema, including when it contains zero rows.

Subsequent processed batches must have matching field names, field order, Arrow types, and nullability. Schema metadata differences are ignored.

An incompatible batch raises ValueError before being passed to the sink. ETLRelay does not automatically cast values, reorder fields, or reconcile incompatible schemas.

docs.title: Output files and transactions
docs.text:
Local file output uses truncating write mode. An existing output file is truncated when it is opened for writing, and a failed operation may leave an empty or partially written file.

An entirely empty pipeline source does not invoke the sink, so it does not truncate an existing output file through FileSink.

SQL output is append-only. Each nonempty batch is written in its own transaction. A failed transaction is rolled back according to the database and SQLAlchemy transaction behavior, but previously committed batches remain committed.

ETLRelay does not provide atomic file replacement, pipeline-wide transactions, automatic retries, or rollback of all previously written output.

docs.title: Resource cleanup
docs.text:
File streams acquired by FileSource and FileSink are closed when their operations complete or fail.

Pipeline attempts to close active processing and source iterators on termination when they expose callable close() methods.

Configuration-built pipelines use a shared SqlEngineFactory managed by PipelineBuilder. The caller must close the builder after execution, including when execution raises an exception.

Direct Python SQL components borrow their supplied engines; the application retains responsibility for disposing of those engines.

For detailed contracts, see Pipeline, File Sink, TabularReader and TabularWriter, and SQL Source and Sink.

docs.title: Complete runnable examples
docs.text:
The repository's examples/configuration/ directory contains nine schema-v1 YAML files for the combinations above, a reusable runner, a data-preparation script, and input setup for local CSV, Parquet, and SQLite. See Getting Started for setup and run commands. The examples use a small schema with id, amount, and state columns; the pipeline selects id and amount, filters amount >= 0, and renames id to record_id.

  • Example runner
  • Prepare example data
  • Configuration examples directory

The examples expect commands to be run from the repository root so relative paths are interpreted consistently. The SQL examples require the environment variables shown below to point at the SQLite demo databases created by prepare_demo_data.py:

export ETLRELAY_SOURCE_DATABASE_URL="sqlite:///examples/configuration/data/source.db"
export ETLRELAY_SINK_DATABASE_URL="sqlite:///examples/configuration/data/sink.db"

Only examples that use SQL need the corresponding variable. The values above are non-secret local SQLite URLs; real connection URLs may contain credentials and must not be placed directly in YAML.

docs.title: Environment variables and secrets
docs.text:
The configuration stores the environment-variable name, not the resolved URL. For example, connection_url_env: ETLRELAY_SOURCE_DATABASE_URL tells the builder which environment variable to resolve.

  • Set required variables in the process environment before building a SQL pipeline.
  • Missing and empty variable values cause preflight to fail before ETL component factories are invoked or source/sink I/O begins.
  • Each unique referenced variable is resolved once during preflight.
  • Error messages identify the configuration path and variable name, but must not include the resolved URL or credentials.
  • Never put passwords, tokens, or credential-bearing connection URLs directly in YAML examples or commit them to version control.

Environment variables provide secret indirection, not a dedicated secrets vault. Deployment-specific secret injection, access control, rotation, and environment hygiene remain the application's responsibility. See Security.

docs.title: Validation and representative errors
docs.text:
Validation rejects malformed documents and unsupported configuration before runtime construction. Examples of actionable error messages include:

Problem Example message Unsupported schema version version must be the integer 1. Missing root field Required top-level field 'processors' is missing. Unsupported property sink.destination is not a supported field. Unsupported format source.format 'xlsx' is not supported for reading. Invalid filter operator processors[0].operator must be one of '==', '!=', '<', '<=', '>', '>='. Missing SQL environment variable source.connection_url_env references missing or empty environment variable 'ETLRELAY_SOURCE_DATABASE_URL'.

The full SQL preflight error is wrapped in PipelineBuildError; it may aggregate multiple missing references into one message. Component validators normally return lists of path-qualified errors; the root ConfigValidator raises ConfigurationError containing those validation errors.

YAML syntax/document errors are distinct from schema errors. YamlReader rejects malformed YAML, duplicate mapping keys, and multiple documents with yaml.YAMLError. It raises YamlDocumentError (a ValueError subclass) for an empty document, a non-mapping root, or non-string root keys. ConfigLoader does not translate filesystem or reader exceptions into ConfigurationError by default.

Validation does not guarantee that source files exist, SQL parses or executes, destination tables exist, columns match the data, or output operations will succeed. Those conditions depend on runtime components and external resources.

docs.title: Schema security and scope
docs.text:
• YAML is parsed with a safe loader; arbitrary Python object construction is not part of configuration loading.
  • The default CLI resolves component types through explicit built-in registries. Applications may deliberately compose their own registries in Python; YAML does not discover or import them. Schema v1 does not provide dynamic imports, user code evaluation, or arbitrary plugin loading.
  • SQL text remains caller-authored SQL. Bind values rather than interpolating untrusted values, and validate/allowlist dynamic identifiers separately.
  • Local path validation is a containment check, not a full OS sandbox or authorization policy.
  • JSON configuration, remote storage, additional formats/processors, dynamic plugin loading, schema migrations, and SQL table-creation modes are outside the frozen v1.0 scope. The CLI supports the same built-in schema described here.

docs.title: Development
docs.text:
ETLRelay uses Nix flakes for its development environment, uv for Python dependencies and lockfiles, pytest for tests, Ruff for linting and formatting, Pyright for static typing, MkDocs for documentation, GitHub Actions for CI, and PyPI for distribution.

Python 3.12 is the default development interpreter. ETLRelay supports CPython 3.12, 3.13, and 3.14.

docs.title: Development environment
docs.text:
Enter the Nix development shell:

nix develop

The shell provides Python 3.12, 3.13, and 3.14, along with the configured development tooling. Node.js is provided for Pyright.

The repository's .python-version selects Python 3.12 by default.

Synchronize the committed lockfile and all dependency groups:

uv sync --python 3.12 --locked --all-groups

Python 3.12 remains the baseline for development, Ruff, Pyright, and the full CI quality checks.

Other supported interpreter versions are used for compatibility testing without changing the project's primary development environment.

docs.title: Dependency integrity
docs.text:
Verify that the lockfile matches project metadata:

uv lock --check

Audit locked dependencies:

uv audit --locked --preview-features audit-command

Check the installed environment:

uv pip check --python .venv/bin/python

The vulnerability audit includes runtime and development dependency groups. An archived dependency may be reported as an adverse project status without being a known vulnerability.

A successful audit does not establish that dependencies are free from undiscovered vulnerabilities.

When changing dependencies, regenerate and review uv.lock. Prefer targeted dependency updates when resolving a specific security advisory.

docs.title: Quality checks
docs.text:
Run the full test suite with statement and branch coverage:

uv run pytest \
    --cov=etlrelay \
    --cov-branch \
    --cov-report=term-missing \
    --cov-report=xml \
    --cov-fail-under=90.1

The configured minimum coverage is 90.1%. The coverage threshold is enforced by CI.

Run linting, formatting, type checking, and documentation validation:

uv run ruff check src tests
uv run ruff format --check src tests
uv run pyright
uv run mkdocs build --strict

For Python 3.12 compatibility, keep the configured Ruff and Pyright language targets aligned with the minimum supported Python version.

docs.title: Build and verify distributions
docs.text:
Remove previous build artifacts and build the source distribution and wheel:

rm -rf dist
uv build

Validate the distribution metadata:

uvx --from 'twine>=7,<8' twine check dist/*

Verify the packaged modules, metadata, runtime dependency declarations, and CLI entry point:

uv run python tests/packaging/check_distributions.py

The distribution verification checks the built archives, not just the repository source tree.

This does not replace installed-artifact testing: a valid archive can still contain runtime or dependency errors.

docs.title: Installed-artifact compatibility
docs.text:
The compatibility smoke test installs both the wheel and source distribution into separate clean virtual environments outside the repository checkout. Source installation uses an isolated build from the archive.

It verifies public imports, dependency consistency, direct CSV/Parquet/SQLite pipelines, CLI version/help output, YAML validation, and a minimal CSV CLI pipeline. Use --artifact wheel or --artifact sdist to select one artifact; the default is both.

Run the checks with the additional supported interpreters:

uv run --no-project --python 3.13 \
    python tests/packaging/smoke_compatibility.py dist

uv run --no-project --python 3.14 \
    python tests/packaging/smoke_compatibility.py dist

Using --no-project prevents these compatibility checks from changing the repository's primary Python 3.12 environment.

The CI workflow tests both artifacts on every declared Python/platform combination, including macOS and Windows. See the packaging verification record for baseline CI evidence, local results, and checks pending CI.

docs.title: CI coverage
docs.text:
The primary CI job runs on Ubuntu with Python 3.12 and checks:

  • Lockfile consistency and dependency security.
  • Installed dependency compatibility.
  • Documentation, tests, coverage, linting, formatting, and types.
  • Wheel and source-distribution builds.
  • Distribution metadata and package contents.
  • Installed CLI behavior and a complete local CSV pipeline.
  • Selected CLI failure codes and sensitive-data disclosure regressions.

The compatibility matrix verifies the same built wheel and source distribution in these additional configurations:

Platform Python Verification Ubuntu 3.13 Wheel and sdist smoke Ubuntu 3.14 Wheel and sdist smoke macOS 3.12 Wheel and sdist smoke Windows 3.12 Wheel and sdist smoke

The full test suite is not repeated for every matrix entry. These jobs verify the installed artifact and a representative execution path.

docs.title: Preview documentation
docs.text:
Start the local documentation server:

uv run mkdocs serve

MkDocs serves a preview and rebuilds pages as source files change.

Build the documentation with warnings treated as errors:

uv run mkdocs build --strict

Generated output is written to site/ and should not be committed.

The API reference uses mkdocstrings to render Python docstrings. When public contracts change, update the relevant source docstrings, API reference, architecture documentation, and user-facing guides.

docs.title: Release verification
docs.text:
Before publishing a new version:

  1. Confirm the intended version and supported Python range in pyproject.toml.
  2. Regenerate and verify uv.lock.
  3. Update the changelog, README, documentation homepage, and versioned documentation links.
  4. Run dependency checks and the full quality suite.
  5. Build fresh distribution artifacts and validate their contents.
  6. Test both built artifacts in separate clean environments outside the repository checkout.
  7. Confirm the CI quality job and compatibility matrix pass.
  8. Review the changeset for unintended API, dependency, or behavioral changes.
  9. Follow the documented TestPyPI and production publication workflow.
  10. Verify the published package, GitHub release, and versioned documentation.

See Release Automation and the repository's RELEASE_CHECKS.md for the release procedure and acceptance records.

A successful editable installation is not evidence that the wheel or source distribution is correct.

docs.title: Development principles
docs.text:
ETLRelay follows incremental, test-driven development:

  1. Establish the requirement and acceptance criteria.
  2. Add focused tests.
  3. Implement the minimum behavior needed.
  4. Refactor without changing verified contracts.
  5. Run quality and regression checks.
  6. Update relevant documentation.

Prefer explicit component contracts and small abstractions. Avoid introducing new architectural layers without a demonstrated requirement.

docs.title: Contributing
docs.text:
Base focused pull requests on dev. During the feature freeze, changes must address correctness, security, compatibility, or release readiness; propose other features separately for post-v1.0 review.

For a defect, include the affected version/commit, expected and observed behavior, and a minimal reproduction with synthetic data. Add focused regression coverage and update the relevant user guide and source docstrings. Run the test, quality, documentation, dependency, and packaging checks above before review. Use the private reporting procedure in the repository's SECURITY.md for suspected vulnerabilities rather than posting sensitive details publicly.

Executable documentation is checked by tests/functional/test_cli_installed.py::test_installed_candidate_runs_documented_examples. It runs the quick-start snippets and repository examples against an installed wheel outside the checkout. Update its expected outputs when an intentional example change alters behavior. Do not substitute an editable install for this check.

docs.title: Extending through Python protocols
docs.text:
An application can pass its own Source, Processor, Sink, tabular reader, writer, or filesystem implementation directly to the corresponding constructors. No inheritance or registration is required for direct Python composition. Respect the documented signatures, schema compatibility, and resource ownership.

examples/custom_processor.py implements UppercaseNames.process(batch) -> Batch using Arrow, then supplies it to Pipeline alongside the built-in CSV source and sink. It preserves field types/nullability and propagates invalid input errors. Run it with the installed candidate:

python examples/custom_processor.py

The existing explicit registry/factory/validator types also support deliberate application composition, as described in the registry reference. Such registrations do not modify the default CLI catalog. Automatic plugin discovery and YAML-driven arbitrary imports remain unsupported. Keep custom components trusted, document their failure/cleanup behavior, and test them independently.

docs.title: Getting Started
docs.text: This guide covers ETLRelay v1.0.0. Applications upgrading from v0.9.0 need no Python or YAML changes. For older versions, see the v0.9.0 migration guide.

docs.title: Install in a clean environment
docs.text:
Use CPython 3.12, 3.13, or 3.14. Create and activate a virtual environment:

python -m venv .venv

On Linux/macOS, run source .venv/bin/activate. On Windows PowerShell, run .venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1. Run the remaining commands in that environment.

Install the release and inspect its commands:

python -m pip install etlrelay==1.0.0
etlrelay --help
etlrelay version

etlrelay version reports etlrelay 1.0.0. To verify a local release build before publication, run uv build in the checkout and install its archive in the clean environment instead:

python -m pip install /absolute/path/to/ETLRelay/dist/etlrelay-1.0.0-py3-none-any.whl

docs.title: Run a self-contained CSV pipeline
docs.text:
In a writable working directory, save this as input.csv:

id,amount,state
1,10,ready
2,-2,skip
3,5,ready

Save this as pipeline.yaml in the same directory:

version: 1
source:
  type: file
  path: input.csv
  format: csv
  storage:
    type: local
    base_path: .
processors:
  - type: select_columns
    columns: [id, amount]
  - type: filter_rows
    column: amount
    operator: ">"
    value: 0
  - type: rename_columns
    mapping:
      id: record_id
sink:
  type: file
  path: output.csv
  format: csv
  storage:
    type: local
    base_path: .

Validate, then execute from that directory:

etlrelay validate pipeline.yaml
etlrelay run pipeline.yaml

validate parses and checks the document/schema. It does not build runtime components, resolve SQL connection values, or run data processing. Successful validation does not prove that input data or output resources will work.

A successful run prints Pipeline completed: pipeline.yaml and creates:

"record_id","amount"
1,10
3,5

All four root fields are required. processors: [] is valid. The integer version: 1 is the configuration schema version, independent of the package version. Formats are selected explicitly rather than inferred from extensions.

docs.title: Compose the equivalent pipeline in Python
docs.text:
Save this as pipeline.py beside the same input.csv:

from pathlib import Path

from etlrelay.pipeline import Pipeline
from etlrelay.processors import FilterRows, RenameColumns, SelectColumns
from etlrelay.readers import CsvReader
from etlrelay.security import PathValidator
from etlrelay.sinks import FileSink
from etlrelay.sources import FileSource
from etlrelay.storage import LocalFileSystem
from etlrelay.writers import CsvWriter

storage = LocalFileSystem(PathValidator(Path.cwd()))
Pipeline(
    FileSource("input.csv", storage, CsvReader()),
    [
        SelectColumns(["id", "amount"]),
        FilterRows("amount", ">", 0),
        RenameColumns({"id": "record_id"}),
    ],
    FileSink("python-output.csv", storage, CsvWriter()),
).run()

Run python pipeline.py. python-output.csv contains the same records and columns as output.csv.

A pipeline entirely without batches leaves its destination untouched. Opening a local output otherwise truncates existing contents; failures may leave partial output. SQL sinks append to existing tables using one transaction per nonempty batch. Neither path provides pipeline-wide rollback.

docs.title: Run the repository examples
docs.text:
Obtain the examples/ directory from the v1.0.0 release tag. A published package should instead use examples from its matching release tag. Examples are repository files, not a guaranteed wheel payload.

From a repository root or a working directory containing a copied examples/:

python examples/copy_csv.py
python examples/transform_csv.py
python examples/parquet_pipeline.py
python examples/sqlite_pipeline.py
python examples/custom_processor.py
python examples/configuration/prepare_demo_data.py
etlrelay run examples/configuration/csv_to_csv.yaml

The preparation script recreates demonstration tables. It is for disposable demo resources, not an application migration tool. See the YAML examples instructions for all nine configurations, SQL environment setup, expected results, and reset behavior.

The SQL examples use local SQLite URLs without credentials. Real SQL components reference environment-variable names, not literal URLs in YAML. The destination table must already exist. Missing or empty variables fail during run build preflight; validate does not resolve them.

docs.title: Troubleshoot the first run
docs.text:
Symptom Check Command is unavailable Activate the environment where the archive was installed; inspect etlrelay version. Exit 2 Check command syntax and required arguments with etlrelay help run. Exit 3 Check YAML shape/schema, supported fields, configuration-file access, and build-time SQL environment references. Exit 4 Check input parsing, selected columns/types, filesystem access, existing SQL tables, and cleanup. Earlier output may remain. Exit 1 An unexpected internal failure occurred; reproduce with synthetic data and report the version/commit and operation. A relative path cannot be found Paths use the process working directory and configured storage base, not the YAML file's directory. Diagnostics need more context Run etlrelay --log-level debug run pipeline.yaml; logs go to stderr and omit raw runtime exception details.

See Configuration, CLI Reference, Logging, and Security for precise contracts and Migration to v0.9.0 for API changes.

docs.title: Logging
docs.text:
ETLRelay uses Python's standard-library logging module to provide operational visibility into pipeline execution, configuration validation, file and SQL operations, and resource management.

Logging is configurable through the CLI or through standard Python logging configuration when ETLRelay is used as a library.

ETLRelay does not require an external logging dependency or introduce its own logging framework.

docs.title: CLI logging
docs.text:
Use the global --log-level option to control logging verbosity:

etlrelay --log-level info run pipeline.yaml

The option is available to CLI commands and must appear before the command name.

For example:

etlrelay --log-level debug run pipeline.yaml
etlrelay --log-level info validate pipeline.yaml
etlrelay --log-level warning run pipeline.yaml

The default logging level is WARNING.

docs.title: Supported logging levels
docs.text:
Level Description DEBUG Detailed operational events, including component lifecycle, processing progress, and resource management INFO High-level pipeline execution events, including start and successful completion WARNING Secondary or recoverable operational failures, such as resource cleanup failures ERROR Unexpected operational failures requiring attention CRITICAL Reserved for critical failures; ETLRelay does not currently define routine critical-level events

Logging levels are case-insensitive.

An unsupported level is rejected as a CLI argument error.

docs.title: Example: INFO logging
docs.text:
Run a pipeline with informational logging:

etlrelay --log-level info run pipeline.yaml

A successful execution produces lifecycle messages similar to:

INFO etlrelay.pipeline.pipeline: Pipeline execution started.
INFO etlrelay.pipeline.pipeline: Pipeline execution completed.

The CLI continues to report normal command results separately from log messages.

docs.title: Example: DEBUG logging
docs.text:
Use DEBUG to inspect additional operational activity:

etlrelay --log-level debug run pipeline.yaml

Depending on the configured pipeline, additional events can include:

DEBUG etlrelay.config.loader: Configuration loading started.
DEBUG etlrelay.config.loader: Configuration validation completed.
DEBUG etlrelay.config.pipeline_builder: Pipeline components resolved.
DEBUG etlrelay.config.pipeline_builder: Pipeline construction completed.
DEBUG etlrelay.sources.file: File source read started.
DEBUG etlrelay.pipeline.pipeline: Processed batch 1: 100 rows.
DEBUG etlrelay.sources.file: File source read completed.
DEBUG etlrelay.sinks.file: File sink write completed.

These examples are illustrative. The events produced depend on the components used and whether execution completes successfully.

DEBUG provides more operational detail; it does not enable logging of data records, SQL parameters, or credentials.

docs.title: Standard output and standard error
docs.text:
ETLRelay separates normal command output from operational logs:

  • stdout contains normal CLI output, such as successful command results.
  • stderr contains logging messages and CLI error diagnostics.

This separation allows normal output to be redirected independently from diagnostics.

For example:

etlrelay --log-level info run pipeline.yaml > result.txt 2> pipeline.log

The command redirects normal output to result.txt and logs or error messages to pipeline.log.

ETLRelay's CLI logging configuration applies for the duration of the command. It does not permanently reconfigure the application's root logger.

docs.title: Python library logging
docs.text:
When ETLRelay is used directly through its Python API, the calling application controls logging configuration.

ETLRelay modules use named loggers under the etlrelay namespace, such as:

  • etlrelay.pipeline.pipeline
  • etlrelay.sources.file
  • etlrelay.sinks.file
  • etlrelay.sources.sql
  • etlrelay.sinks.sql
  • etlrelay.config.loader
  • etlrelay.config.pipeline_builder
  • etlrelay.config.sql_engine_factory
  • etlrelay.writers.parquet

A standalone Python application can enable logging using the standard library:

import logging

logging.basicConfig(
    level=logging.INFO,
    format="%(levelname)s %(name)s: %(message)s",
)

# Construct and execute an ETLRelay pipeline.
pipeline.run()

Here, pipeline represents a previously constructed ETLRelay Pipeline.

The application may instead configure the etlrelay logger specifically, use its existing logging handlers, or integrate logging with its own observability system.

Importing ETLRelay does not configure the application's root logger or force a particular logging destination or format.

docs.title: Pipeline execution
docs.text:
Pipeline emits:

Level Event Meaning INFO Pipeline execution started. Pipeline execution has begun INFO Pipeline execution completed. Pipeline execution finished successfully DEBUG Processed batch N: X rows. Batch N passed processor execution and pipeline schema validation

An empty source can complete successfully without producing any batches.

A processed-batch event does not guarantee that the sink has committed or persisted that batch. Persistence is the responsibility of the sink.

If execution fails, the successful-completion event is not emitted.

docs.title: File sources and sinks
docs.text:
File components emit DEBUG lifecycle events:

Component Events FileSource Read started; read completed FileSink Write started; write completed

Read completion is reported after normal iteration finishes and the source stream closes.

Write completion is reported after serialization succeeds and the output stream closes.

Failures do not produce successful-completion events. An early-closed source iterator does not report normal read completion.

docs.title: SQL sources and sinks
docs.text:
SQL components emit DEBUG events for successful operations.

SqlSource reports the number of rows successfully retrieved and converted into an ETLRelay batch.

SqlSink reports successful batch commits, including the number of inserted rows.

A SQL sink commit event is emitted after the batch transaction commits successfully. A transaction that fails or rolls back does not produce a successful-commit event.

Each nonempty SQL sink batch uses its own transaction. Successfully committed earlier batches remain committed if a later batch fails.

docs.title: Configuration and SQL resources
docs.text:
Configuration components emit DEBUG events when:

  • Configuration loading starts.
  • Configuration validation completes successfully.
  • Pipeline component registrations resolve.
  • Required SQL connection environment preflight succeeds.
  • Pipeline construction completes successfully.

The SQL engine factory also emits events when owned engines are created, reused from its cache, or successfully disposed.

These events do not include resolved connection URLs or credentials.

docs.title: Errors and failure reporting
docs.text: ETLRelay distinguishes operational logging from exception handling.

docs.title: Exception precedence and cleanup logging
docs.text:
ETLRelay distinguishes an operation's primary failure from secondary failures encountered while releasing resources.

When Pipeline.run() terminates, it attempts to close the active processing iterator and underlying source iterator when they expose callable close() methods.

If pipeline execution raises an exception, that exception remains primary even when iterator cleanup also fails. Secondary cleanup failures are reported using controlled warning messages that identify the exception type without including the original exception message.

If execution otherwise succeeds but iterator cleanup fails, the first cleanup exception propagates after cleanup has been attempted for the remaining closeable iterators.

Successful pipeline completion is not logged when required cleanup fails.

ParquetWriter also preserves a serialization/upstream error if footer finalization fails. Its warning is Parquet writer cleanup failed (TYPE).; exception messages are omitted. A finalization-only failure propagates and can leave unreadable output. See stream contracts.

SQL sink batch-commit messages are emitted only after the corresponding transaction context has exited successfully. A failed commit must not be reported as successful.

These logging behaviors do not replace Python exception handling. Direct Python callers may still receive underlying exceptions containing information from external libraries. ETLRelay does not attempt to sanitize arbitrary third-party exceptions observed by calling applications.

docs.title: Python API
docs.text:
ETLRelay generally propagates underlying exceptions to Python callers rather than wrapping every failure in a generic framework exception.

Specific boundaries may translate errors where doing so provides a clearer contract. Examples include configuration validation, SQL environment preflight, and missing input-file handling.

Logging does not change the original exception or the caller's responsibility for handling it.

docs.title: CLI
docs.text:
The CLI reports validation, construction, execution, and cleanup failures using its established error-handling and exit-code conventions.

Unexpected failures can be logged with the failing operation and exception class without including the raw exception message.

If execution and resource cleanup both fail, the execution failure remains primary. Cleanup problems may be reported separately as warnings.

A failed operation is never logged as successfully completed.

For command syntax and exit-code details, consult the CLI help:

etlrelay --help
etlrelay run --help
etlrelay validate --help

docs.title: Sensitive information and logging
docs.text:
ETLRelay's built-in operational logging is designed to provide useful diagnostics without routinely exposing sensitive application data.

The standard logging events do not include:

  • Complete data batches or record values.
  • SQL query text or bound query parameters.
  • Database connection URLs, passwords, or credentials.
  • Access tokens or other secrets from SQL connection configuration.
  • Full configuration payloads.
  • Raw third-party exception messages or tracebacks.

Log messages focus on operational stages, component lifecycles, row counts, and exception types.

The DEBUG level does not disable these restrictions.

docs.title: Security boundaries and limitations
docs.text:
These protections apply to logging and CLI output controlled by ETLRelay. They are not a universal guarantee that no sensitive information can appear in application diagnostics.

Important limitations include:

  • Direct Python callers receive underlying exceptions, which may contain database statements, parameter values, file paths, or driver-specific details.
  • External libraries and database drivers may have independent logging configurations.
  • Application-provided logging handlers and custom components may record additional information.
  • Explicitly enabling SQLAlchemy statement or parameter logging can expose sensitive SQL data.
  • ETLRelay does not attempt to sanitize arbitrary third-party exception messages through a general-purpose redaction framework.

Applications remain responsible for protecting log files, configuring appropriate log retention and access controls, and managing database credentials securely.

For additional information about security responsibilities and limitations, see Security.

docs.title: No INFO messages appear
docs.text:
The default logging level is WARNING. Enable informational logging explicitly:

etlrelay --log-level info run pipeline.yaml

docs.title: More operational detail is needed
docs.text:
Use DEBUG:

etlrelay --log-level debug run pipeline.yaml

This provides additional component and batch-level diagnostics without enabling payload logging.

docs.title: A pipeline fails without a detailed traceback
docs.text:
The CLI intentionally avoids printing potentially sensitive raw exception details.

For application-level investigation, use ETLRelay's Python API where appropriate and handle the underlying exception within your application's own error-reporting and security policy.

docs.title: SQL operations are not visible in logs
docs.text:
ETLRelay's SQL operational events generally use DEBUG. Enable that level to see successful source reads, batch commits, and engine lifecycle events.

ETLRelay does not automatically enable SQLAlchemy's SQL statement logging.

docs.title: Duplicate logging messages appear in a Python application
docs.text:
Check whether the application has configured multiple handlers for the same logger or has allowed messages to propagate to handlers higher in the logger hierarchy.

The ETLRelay library does not install its own application-wide logging handlers.

docs.title: ETLRelay Roadmap
docs.text:
ETLRelay is a lightweight Python library and CLI for repeatable tabular ETL jobs. Post-v1.0 development expands the jobs users can complete: common databases, files and cloud storage; useful transformations; repeatable loads; and convenient, explicit configuration. The library and CLI remain independently usable.

ETLRelay v1.0.0 establishes the stable release of the reviewed v0.9.0 runtime, YAML schema version 1, and documented Python/CLI interfaces. See the release record for verification and release details. Planned additions below are outside the v1.0 support policy until implemented and released.

docs.title: Release summary
docs.text:
Version Status Delivered outcome 0.1.0 / 0.1.x Released Initial Arrow-backed batch pipeline, local CSV workflows, and stabilization 0.2.0 Released Batch/schema contracts and select, rename, and filter processors 0.3.0 Released Parquet input/output through the file composition model 0.4.0 Released Local storage, path, stream ownership, and failure contracts 0.5.0 Released SQL query sources and append-only sinks; SQLite verification 0.6.0 Released Versioned YAML configuration, validation, explicit registrations, and pipeline construction 0.7.0 Released Installed CLI for validation, execution, help, and version reporting 0.8.0 Released Security/operational controls, logging, cleanup, and artifact/compatibility checks 0.9.0 Released Feature freeze, tabular protocol naming, API review, and pipeline/failure/documentation verification 1.0.0 Released Stable compatibility policy and completed release documentation; runtime behavior retained from 0.9.0

Earlier milestone detail is retained in the tagged v0.9.0 roadmap and Git history. The maintained roadmap below governs post-v1.0 development.

docs.title: Post-v1.0.0 roadmap
docs.text:
