This is the selected development direction, researched on 21 October 2026. Minor-version labels describe intended release themes and order, not dates, current capabilities, or a promise to support every version of a technology. Create focused implementation tickets before starting a milestone. Split a milestone when its independently useful parts warrant separate releases; record any scope or ordering changes rather than silently dropping selected work.

The plan extends beyond connectors. More destinations help adoption, but users also need transformations, realistic file layouts, and repeatable loading. Integration breadth must come with maintained installation instructions, representative examples, and reproducible verification.

docs.title: Selected milestones
docs.text:
Target User outcome and selected scope Main completion boundary / dependencies 1.1 — SQL scale and PostgreSQL Opt-in chunked SQL reads; verified PostgreSQL source/sink support Stable cross-chunk schemas, driver buffering, early termination, cleanup, types and per-batch commits tested against a real PostgreSQL service. Preserve existing defaults. 1.2 — Practical transformations Column casting; fill/drop nulls; string cleanup; date parsing; derived columns; richer explicit filters Arrow-backed operations with documented null, overflow, timezone and invalid-value behavior. Restricted declarative operations, including membership, null tests and Boolean predicate composition; no arbitrary code evaluation. 1.3 — Directory inputs and file consolidation Read multiple files from a directory, select filenames with a regular expression, and combine their batches into one destination Deterministic discovery/order; explicit recursion and no-match behavior; consistent format/schema; per-file cleanup and failure propagation. Verify multiple CSV/Parquet inputs to one output file or SQL destination through Python, YAML and CLI. 1.4 — S3 and MySQL-family databases S3 filesystem; verified MySQL and MariaDB reads/writes Reuse SQL/storage contracts from 1.1. Test MySQL and MariaDB separately, using named driver/server versions. Verify cloud credentials, seekable Parquet reads, interrupted writes and cleanup. 1.5 — Business data interchange Verified SQL Server; optional .xlsx reading/writing; deterministic filename-based format inference Document driver/native installation and database type/transaction behavior. Define sheets, headers, dates, formulas versus cached values, and multi-batch workbook output. Explicit format wins; ambiguous suffixes fail clearly. 1.6 — JSON and Arrow interchange JSON mapping configuration; tabular JSON Lines/NDJSON read/write; JSON array-of-records input; Arrow IPC/Feather v2 read/write Keep mapping configuration separate from row data. Define schema, nesting, decimal/time serialization, empty data and bounded parsing. JSON-array input needs a suitable incremental parser; NDJSON output needs an explicitly tested serializer. 1.7 — Trusted component extensions Explicitly enabled, installed custom source/processor/sink/storage/format components through the stock CLI Existing Python composition/registries remain valid. Define extension names, validation/factories, collision policy, dependency diagnostics and compatibility tests. Configuration cannot silently import arbitrary executable code. 1.8 — Partitioned datasets Extend the file-collection source from 1.3 with partitioned Parquet datasets; projection/filter pushdown where supported; compression options; explicit input schemas Builds on directory discovery from 1.3, remote storage adapters and schema work. Define deterministic discovery, partition columns, file sizing, incompatible files, ordering, overwrite/collision rules and partial-dataset cleanup. Compression belongs to the appropriate format/stream layer. 1.9 — Azure and Google Cloud storage Azure Blob Storage/ADLS Gen2 and Google Cloud Storage filesystem adapters Reuse the remote storage behavior verified for S3. Test each service independently, including authentication, prefix boundaries, retries inherited from clients, seekability and failed uploads. Backend/Python/platform support may be narrower than the core package. 1.10 — Enterprise destinations and write modes Verified Oracle support; explicit append, upsert and overwrite modes; opt-in destination-table creation; staged local-file replacement Verify Oracle queries/types/reflection/transactions using a selected driver and real database. Introduce SQL modes first for SQLite/PostgreSQL, then other dialects explicitly. Publish a destination/format capability matrix. Define keys, duplicate/null keys, schema/type creation, one-time overwrite initialization, rollback and partial commits. Local replacement guarantees require same-filesystem staging; do not promise atomic publication on every storage backend. 1.11 — HTTP/API ingestion HTTPS file input and a paginated REST JSON-record source Depends on tabular record conversion from 1.6. Support explicit record paths, selected pagination modes, credential references, timeouts, request/page limits and bounded read retries. Prevent credential forwarding to untrusted pagination/redirect hosts. No universal SaaS connector or HTTP write retry guarantee. 1.12 — Incremental jobs Watermark-based SQL/API extraction across runs; explicit persisted load state Depends on load modes and source contracts. Define cursor ties, late data, overlap/replay, successful-state advancement, concurrent-run exclusion and restart behavior. Persist state only after the corresponding output is durable; document duplicate windows rather than claiming exactly-once delivery. 1.13 — Embedded analytical workflows Optional DuckDB source/sink integration and job-level SQL transformations for joins, aggregates, sorting and deduplication Use a maintained execution engine. Establish an explicit whole-job resource/lifecycle boundary, temporary storage, limits and cleanup. Global operations must see all relevant batches, not silently run once per batch. Verify Arrow interchange and actual spill/memory behavior. 1.14 — Cloud warehouses Optional Snowflake and BigQuery integration Separate feasibility/verification tickets per service. Resolve dialect/dependency compatibility, authenticate through supported methods, and fund reproducible account-backed tests. Define query types, supported writes, load costs and transaction boundaries independently; a SQLAlchemy dialect is not proof of equivalent SQL sink semantics.

SQL Server, formats, processors and cloud adapters do not technically require all earlier milestones. This sequence prioritizes reusable contracts and complete user workflows; independent work can proceed without manufacturing unnecessary dependencies. The higher-risk stateful/analytical milestones require a design review before implementation, while preserving the stable v1 interfaces.

docs.title: Directory inputs and consolidation
docs.text:
Reading a directory of files into one destination is selected for 1.3, before partitioned datasets. The initial implementation supports local CSV/Parquet collections, with remote discovery added alongside the corresponding adapters. A job selects one input directory and an optional filename regex, reads matching files as one ordered stream of batches, applies its processor chain, and writes to one sink. That sink may produce a single output file or write to a SQL table.

  • Validate the regex before opening source files or the destination. Define full-match filename semantics; directory recursion must be explicitly enabled.
  • Discover regular files in a deterministic order and define no-match behavior. Reject a destination that is also selected as an input.
  • Use a common configured format and compatible schema. Format inference, when available, must not silently combine incompatible formats or schemas.
  • Consume files incrementally and release each stream on completion or failure; do not materialize every file or open all streams at once.
  • Feed the entire collection to one sink execution. Do not reopen/truncate the destination for each input file or repeat output headers between input files.
  • Test empty files, zero-row batches, schema differences, invalid regexes, inaccessible files, failure in a later file, cleanup and partial output.

The initial collection source concatenates compatible rows. It does not join records, deduplicate globally or reconcile incompatible schemas automatically.

docs.title: Destination write modes
docs.text:
The target public write-mode vocabulary is append, upsert, overwrite. Support is explicit per destination, format and backend. Unsupported combinations must fail clearly before destination modification; there is no silent fallback.

Mode Intended behavior Required contract append Add incoming rows while retaining existing destination data Define schema compatibility, duplicate handling and format-specific append support. SQL append retains the existing per-batch transaction contract unless a separate option changes it. upsert Insert new keys and update matching keys Require explicit key columns and define duplicate/null keys, update columns, conflicts and transaction boundaries. Initial support targets SQL sinks; keyed file updates are not implied. overwrite Replace the destination's data with the complete output of this job Initialize replacement once per job, across all batches and source files. Define empty-job behavior, metadata preservation, failures and partial publication. Replacing table data does not implicitly authorize dropping/recreating the table.

SQL initially targets all three modes on individually verified backends. File support follows the format/storage capability matrix: CSV append must handle headers correctly; a single Parquet file cannot be appended by concatenating serialized bytes. Partitioned-dataset append has separate file-collision and schema rules. Document unsupported modes for spreadsheets, objects and warehouses instead of assuming that every sink offers every mode.

Existing v1.0 defaults remain compatible: SQL appends, while local file output truncates an existing destination. Staged local-file overwrite is an opt-in stronger publication behavior until deliberately selected by callers. Define cleanup and same-filesystem replacement guarantees; cloud publication must not inherit local atomicity claims.

docs.title: Processor boundaries
docs.text:
The first processor expansion targets operations that correctly transform one Batch at a time. Proposed configuration concepts include casting named columns, replacing nulls, trimming/normalizing strings, parsing dates, calculating columns from named arithmetic/string/date operations, and combining explicit predicates. Public names and constructor signatures are decided in the implementation review.

Do not call per-batch deduplication, sorting, aggregation or ranking a whole-job operation. Forward/backward filling also needs explicit cross-batch semantics. Global joins, group-by, sorting and deduplication belong in the analytical milestone's separate execution boundary. They must not require breaking Processor.process(batch) -> Batch or creating a new distributed engine.

docs.title: Data representations and schemas
docs.text:
A JSON/YAML mapping document describes one configuration object. A JSON array of row mappings or an NDJSON stream describes tabular records; neither is a KeyValueReader result. The JSON-record/API milestones provide concrete reasons for narrow record-to-Batch and Batch-to-record adapters, with explicit schemas, nulls, nesting and batching. They do not justify a generic conversion framework.

Keep current strict output-schema enforcement as the default. Explicit input schemas and casting allow users to stabilize otherwise ambiguous data; automatic schema evolution or silently widening output schemas is not part of this plan. KeyValueWriter and general mapping-document pipelines remain deferred because none of the selected output workflows requires them.

docs.title: Streaming and repeatability
docs.text:
CSV and Parquet already yield incremental batches. SQL chunking fills a specific finite-input gap. A fetchmany loop alone does not establish bounded end-to-end memory: verify each driver's cursor/buffering behavior and measure representative jobs. SQL chunking must also document its effect on per-batch transactions.

Incremental loading in 1.12 is different: it remembers which records were loaded between runs. Define state ownership and failure recovery explicitly. SDK read retries may be useful; automatically retrying a partially committed pipeline is not safe without a defined replay/idempotency contract. Continuous message/event processing, CDC and exactly-once delivery are separate future decisions.

docs.title: Python compatibility and optional installations
docs.text:
Selected compatibility track: Target CPython 3.15 in the first minor release that passes dependency/artifact/platform checks, aiming for 1.1. PyArrow 23 has no CPython 3.15 wheels; PyArrow 26 publishes them. Upgrade after regression testing, retain Python 3.12–3.14 compatibility, and verify declared environments before changing support claims. This track need not block an otherwise complete feature.

Keep integrations with extra drivers/SDKs optional. Record supported combinations per integration; an optional connector's narrower interpreter range must not silently narrow core ETLRelay support. Prefer maintained Arrow filesystem adapters, SQLAlchemy dialects and existing engine clients over independent connector stacks.

Provide documented installation extras where appropriate, usable examples, a troubleshooting guide and a named driver/server test matrix. Cloud integrations need real service checks as well as deterministic local tests. An emulator or S3-compatible endpoint is verified separately; it does not prove all providers.

docs.title: Research and prioritization findings
docs.text:
The 2026 Stack Overflow survey reports PostgreSQL, SQLite, MySQL, SQL Server and MariaDB among commonly used databases. This supports broadening relational verification beyond SQLite/PostgreSQL/SQL Server. It measures surveyed developer usage, not ETLRelay demand or a complete enterprise ETL market.

Arrow already supplies compute kernels, JSON Lines reading, dataset scanning and partitioning, IPC formats, and S3/Azure/GCS/HDFS filesystem implementations. These make substantial expansion feasible through adapters. Oracle also has an included SQLAlchemy dialect and a Python driver whose Thin mode needs no Oracle Client installation; a maintained real database test environment is still required. ETLRelay still owns configuration, lifecycle, schema, failure and installation guarantees. Arrow JSON reading does not by itself supply a JSON writer or a JSON-array streaming parser.

DuckDB's Arrow integration and external-memory execution make it a useful local analytical target before introducing Spark or a custom parallel runtime. Actual query memory/spill behavior remains workload-dependent and must be measured.

Snowflake and BigQuery are promoted from unspecified future integrations to the selected warehouse milestone, with explicit compatibility and account-test gates. At this review, Snowflake's documented SQLAlchemy requirement is >=2.0.44,<2.1, while ETLRelay's lockfile uses 2.1.5. The core requirement sqlalchemy>=2,<3 permits 2.0, but a resolver-compatible installation is only the start: test supported dependency combinations or choose another maintained integration path before claiming support. BigQuery likewise needs its own write and transaction design rather than an assumption that it behaves like SQLite.

docs.title: Tentative future features — pending feasibility and need
docs.text:
The selected plan now includes processors, JSON records/conversion, additional cloud storage, APIs, incremental loading and warehouse integrations that were previously broadly deferred. The following remain unassigned. Review them against a concrete workflow and a sustainable test/support plan, rather than excluding them permanently or advertising them as available.

Candidate Assessment and next acceptance condition ClickHouse, Redshift, Athena, Trino and Databricks SQL Useful analytical integrations with differing dialects, authentication and write capabilities. Evaluate one service at a time; distinguish query-only support from tested sinks and bulk-loading paths. HDFS Feasible through Arrow, but adds Java/Hadoop native client installation, authentication and service-test costs. Promote when there is a maintained cluster/test image and a clear deployment use case. It does not require distributed ETL execution. Hive Potential SQL integration; establish maintained driver/dialect, authentication and read/write semantics with a reproducible service. Hive-style Parquet partitioning in 1.8 does not imply Hive server support. ORC, Avro, XML, legacy Excel and other formats ORC is a plausible Arrow-based addition; others require format-specific dependencies and schema/record rules. Promote a named format when representative interchange files and maintenance capacity justify it. .xlsx support does not imply .xls, macros or formula evaluation. SFTP/FTP and wider filesystem adapters A maintained fsspec-based bridge may cover useful transfer workflows. Establish credential, seek, publication and failure behavior per backend; an arbitrary protocol string must not imply verified support. Prefer SFTP where secure transfer is required. MongoDB, Elasticsearch and other document stores Potential tabular source/sink adapters, with explicit projection, nested-data mapping and bulk/error semantics. Their popularity alone does not settle the mapping-to-table contract. Redis is not prioritized as a general ETL destination. Spark and other execution engines An optional adapter may serve workloads beyond a single machine. Compare it with the selected local analytical approach; define deployment, schema, ownership and failure boundaries without rebuilding Spark inside ETLRelay. Parallel processing Benchmark native Arrow/DuckDB parallelism first. Add configurable worker execution only for a measured bottleneck with explicit ordering, backpressure, cancellation, state and serialization semantics. Distributed computing, Kafka/event streams and CDC Require separate checkpoint, replay, deployment and delivery contracts. Not implied by finite-batch streaming or watermark loads; no custom distributed runtime is planned. Mapping-document pipelines and KeyValueWriter Remain separate from tabular JSON/API records. Need a concrete document transformation/export workflow before adding public lifecycle or writer abstractions. Unrestricted expressions, automatic schema evolution and general DAG scheduling Broader languages/state/orchestration can alter core guarantees. First establish bounded use cases; prefer integration with existing tools over absorbing their execution platforms.

docs.title: Delivery rules
docs.text:
• Preserve the stable compatibility policy: compatible fixes use patches, additions use minors, and incompatible public changes require a major-version proposal. Keep current defaults until compatible opt-ins ship.
  • Start each feature with a user workflow, acceptance criteria, dependency/test costs and focused implementation tickets. Long-range scope can change through an explicit roadmap decision; it is not a v1.0 release requirement.
  • Verify Python, YAML and CLI workflows, data/schema correctness, cleanup, secret handling, failed writes, installation and version-pinned documentation.
  • Retain failure/partial-write guarantees until a named new mode changes them. Document transaction behavior per database; do not assume universal semantics.
  • Record performance and memory baselines for representative larger jobs. Include useful safe run summaries and actionable component/driver diagnostics with relevant milestones; these are execution diagnostics, not a data-quality engine.
  • Add support claims only after integration and built-artifact checks pass. Update the support record, examples, changelog and release notes together.
  • Use maintainer reproductions without requiring an external user base. Review installation friction, maintenance cost and practical usability after releases.

docs.title: Technical references
docs.text:
Sources were reviewed on 21 October 2026. Dependency capabilities inform feasibility; they do not establish ETLRelay support. Product priority is a maintainer judgment, not a measured adoption forecast.

  • 2026 Stack Overflow database survey.
  • SQLAlchemy included/external dialects and cursor/result streaming.
  • Arrow 23 compute kernels, JSON input, datasets, and filesystems.
  • PyArrow 26 published artifacts.
  • Oracle Python driver installation and Thin mode and Oracle Database Free.
  • DuckDB Python/Arrow integration and memory management.
  • Snowflake SQLAlchemy requirements and Google's BigQuery dialect.
  • dlt incremental loading and merge strategies, as examples of the state/write semantics repeatable ingestion must address.
  • GitHub REST API practices, as a representative API's pagination, credentials and rate-limit concerns.

docs.title: Security
docs.text:
ETLRelay v1.0.0 retains the reviewed security and operational contracts established in earlier releases.

The release includes regression-tested controls for local path containment, safe YAML configuration, SQL parameter handling, connection-secret references, error reporting, operational logging, and resource cleanup. Its CI workflow also checks dependencies and verifies built distribution artifacts.

These controls address specific risks. ETLRelay does not provide a filesystem sandbox, SQL authorization boundary, secrets vault, or general-purpose environment for executing untrusted code.

ETLRelay v1.0.0 provides a stable public contract. Applications remain responsible for evaluating suitability, permissions, and operational safeguards before processing sensitive or production data.

docs.title: Local filesystem paths
docs.text:
PathValidator resolves candidate paths and verifies that their resolved locations remain within the configured base directory.

This check addresses path escapes through:

  • Parent-directory traversal such as ...
  • Absolute paths outside the permitted base.
  • Paths that share a textual prefix with the base but are not descendants.
  • Symbolic links resolving outside the permitted base.

LocalFileSystem validates paths before opening local input or output streams. The validation is based on resolved path containment rather than string-prefix matching.

Path validation does not itself guarantee that a file exists or that the operating system will permit access. The filesystem operation determines whether a read or write succeeds.

docs.title: Security limitations
docs.text:
Path validation is not an operating-system sandbox or an authorization mechanism.

In particular:

  • It does not eliminate time-of-check/time-of-use races if filesystem entries change between validation and opening.
  • It cannot prevent access to resources for which the ETLRelay process already has excessive operating-system permissions.
  • It does not prevent other processes from changing files, directory contents, or symbolic links.
  • It does not enforce quotas, disk-space limits, or file-level access policies beyond the underlying operating system.

Run ETLRelay with only the filesystem permissions it requires. Prefer dedicated input/output directories and restrict modification of those directories by untrusted processes.

docs.title: File writes and overwrite behavior
docs.text:
LocalFileSystem creates output files using binary write mode and truncates existing files when they are opened for writing.

Parent directories are not created automatically.

ETLRelay does not provide atomic output replacement or automatic restoration of previous file contents. A failed write may leave an empty or partially written destination.

Backups, temporary-file replacement strategies, and application-level recovery remain the caller's responsibility when those guarantees are required.

See Path Validator, Local Filesystem, and File Sink.

docs.title: YAML configuration safety
docs.text:
ETLRelay reads configuration through YamlReader, which uses a safe YAML loader.

The reader rejects malformed documents, duplicate mapping keys, unsupported YAML object-construction tags, multiple documents where a single document is expected, non-mapping roots, and non-string root keys.

It does not use arbitrary Python object construction from YAML tags.

ConfigValidator validates the closed, versioned configuration schema. Schema version 1 requires the supported top-level structure and rejects unknown properties, unsupported component types, and unsupported configuration versions.

PipelineBuilder resolves explicit component registrations. Configuration does not support unrestricted Python imports, eval, or arbitrary Python expressions.

docs.title: Validation and preflight boundaries
docs.text:
Configuration loading, validation, component construction, and pipeline execution are separate responsibilities.

Validation rejects known configuration errors before normal pipeline execution. When building a configured pipeline, required SQL connection environment-variable references are checked before component factories are invoked.

These guarantees do not establish that:

  • Referenced files exist, are readable, or contain valid runtime data.
  • SQL connection URLs are valid or databases are reachable.
  • Database users have the required permissions.
  • SQL queries are authorized or return compatible data.
  • Destination tables have compatible schemas or constraints.
  • Custom components are trustworthy.
  • All future runtime failures can be detected in advance.

The CLI validate command does not execute the configured data pipeline or write its output, but it is not a comprehensive security or runtime preflight.

Treat configuration from untrusted sources as untrusted input, even when it satisfies the YAML schema.

See YAML Configuration and Configuration Loading.

docs.title: SQL connection secrets
docs.text:
SQL configuration uses connection_url_env to name an environment variable containing a SQLAlchemy connection URL.

The configuration validator requires a valid environment-variable identifier rather than accepting a literal connection URL in that field.

During PipelineBuilder.build(), required environment-variable references are preflighted. Missing or empty values cause PipelineBuildError before component factories run.

SqlEngineFactory avoids including resolved connection URLs, credentials, or underlying driver exception messages in its own controlled error messages.

Do not commit connection URLs, passwords, API tokens, or private connection information to YAML files, examples, logs, or version control.

docs.title: Environment-variable limitations
docs.text:
Environment variables provide secret indirection, not secure secret storage.

ETLRelay does not provide credential encryption, rotation, access-control policy enforcement, or a secrets vault.

Applications and deployments must protect environment values, process permissions, operational logs, and diagnostic output. Use an appropriate external secrets-management or platform-native credential-injection mechanism where stronger controls are required.

Third-party libraries and application-provided logging handlers may disclose information outside ETLRelay's controlled diagnostics.

docs.title: SQL parameterization and authorization
docs.text:
SqlSource supports SQLAlchemy bound parameters for SQL values. Parameter values are sent as data rather than interpolated into the query string.

Use bound parameters for variable query values. Do not construct SQL by concatenating untrusted values into query text.

SQL identifiers, such as table names and column names, cannot be supplied as ordinary bound values. When dynamically constructing SQL identifiers, use trusted allowlists and appropriate SQLAlchemy APIs.

SqlSink uses SQLAlchemy statement construction and works with existing destination tables. It validates batch column names and uses SQLAlchemy's handling of SQL identifiers.

These behaviors reduce risks associated with unsafe SQL string construction, but they do not establish a SQL authorization policy.

SqlSource accepts caller-authored SQL query text. ETLRelay does not analyze queries to determine whether they are safe, read-only, efficient, or authorized.

The configured database account determines which operations the database permits. Apply least-privilege database credentials and review any SQL accepted from external users.

docs.title: Supported database scope
docs.text:
SQLite is the reference integration-test backend.

Other SQLAlchemy dialects require their corresponding drivers, suitable database permissions, and independent testing.

SqlSink provides append-only writes to existing tables. It does not implement table creation, schema migration, replacement, upserts, or database-level authorization controls.

docs.title: Error handling and logging
docs.text:
ETLRelay uses Python's standard logging module for operational diagnostics.

Built-in logging is intended to describe pipeline execution, validation, batch counts, component activity, and resource lifecycle events without routinely including record contents, SQL parameter values, complete connection URLs, or credentials.

The CLI defaults to WARNING and accepts --log-level to select a supported operational logging level. CLI logs are written to stderr, separately from normal command output.

When ETLRelay is used as a Python library, logging configuration belongs to the calling application. ETLRelay does not configure the application's root logger.

docs.title: Error propagation
docs.text:
Direct Python callers generally receive the original exceptions raised by the relevant components, including third-party exceptions where applicable.

The CLI separates usage errors, configuration and construction failures, and execution failures using documented exit codes:

Exit code Meaning 0 Successful execution 1 Unexpected CLI failure 2 Command usage error 3 Configuration or pipeline construction failure 4 Pipeline execution or cleanup failure

For unexpected operational failures, the CLI avoids displaying raw third-party exception messages that could contain sensitive connection information or payloads.

Secondary iterator-cleanup failures are logged using controlled diagnostics rather than their exception messages.

docs.title: Redaction boundaries
docs.text:
These protections apply to ETLRelay-controlled logging and CLI diagnostics, not every possible diagnostic produced by a process.

They do not guarantee that all sensitive information is removed from:

  • Exceptions observed by direct Python callers.
  • Custom sources, processors, sinks, readers, or writers.
  • Third-party database drivers and SQLAlchemy logging.
  • Application-installed logging handlers.
  • External monitoring and error-reporting services.
  • User-supplied values intentionally included in configuration errors or application logs.

Avoid logging raw records, environment dumps, connection URLs, or SQL query payloads in production environments. Configure external library logging and diagnostic collection with the same care as ETLRelay's built-in logging.

See Logging for operational levels, supported events, and further limitations.

docs.title: Resource ownership and cleanup
docs.text: ETLRelay separates resources owned by a component from resources supplied by a caller.

docs.title: File resources
docs.text:
FileSource owns the input stream obtained from its configured FileSystem. FileSink owns the output stream it opens for writing.

Both use context-managed streams and release them on normal completion and relevant failures.

Readers and writers borrow streams provided by their callers; they do not close those streams.

When Pipeline.run() terminates, it attempts to close the active processing and source iterators when those iterators expose callable close() methods.

This includes early sink termination and failures during source iteration, processing, or writing.

Applications consuming a FileSource generator directly must close an active generator when they stop reading early and require deterministic cleanup.

docs.title: Failure precedence
docs.text:
If pipeline execution fails and iterator cleanup also fails, the original execution exception takes precedence.

Secondary cleanup failures are reported through controlled operational warnings.

If execution otherwise succeeds but required iterator cleanup fails, the first cleanup exception propagates.

The pipeline does not dispose of injected storage backends, database engines, or component instances merely because execution has completed.

docs.title: SQL resources
docs.text:
Direct Python SqlSource and SqlSink instances borrow the SQLAlchemy engine supplied by the caller. The caller remains responsible for engine disposal.

SqlSource manages the connection and query-result resources acquired during reading and releases them on completion or failure.

SqlSink uses an independent transaction for each nonempty batch. Failed transactions are rolled back through SQLAlchemy's transaction context, while previously committed batches remain committed.

Zero-row SQL sink batches are skipped before table reflection, column validation, or transaction creation.

For configuration-built pipelines, PipelineBuilder manages the shared SqlEngineFactory lifecycle. Call builder.close() after execution to release factory-owned engines, including when the pipeline fails.

Do not close a successfully built pipeline's required SQL resources before it runs.

See Pipeline and SQL Source and Sink.

docs.title: Empty data, schemas, and partial output
docs.text:
An entirely empty pipeline source produces no batches, so Pipeline does not invoke its sink.

A zero-row batch is different: it participates in processing and output-schema validation and is passed to the sink.

The first processed batch establishes the pipeline's expected output schema. Subsequent batches must match field names, field order, Arrow types, and nullability. Schema metadata differences are ignored.

Incompatible batches raise ValueError before being delivered to the sink.

The concrete writer or sink determines how valid zero-row batches are persisted:

  • CsvWriter can write a header from a schema-bearing zero-row batch.
  • ParquetWriter can write a valid empty Parquet file from a schema-bearing zero-row batch; an entirely empty iterable cannot establish its schema and raises WriterError.
  • SqlSink skips zero-row batches without starting a transaction.

Pipeline execution is not atomic. A later validation or execution failure does not roll back earlier completed file writes or committed SQL batches.

docs.title: Dependency and distribution integrity
docs.text:
The v1.0.0 CI workflow includes:

  • Lockfile consistency verification.
  • Dependency vulnerability auditing.
  • Installed dependency compatibility checks.
  • Wheel and source-distribution builds.
  • Distribution metadata and package-content verification.
  • Separate clean-environment installation of the wheel and source distribution.
  • Installed CLI and representative pipeline smoke tests.
  • Compatibility verification across the documented Python/platform matrix.

These checks help identify packaging mistakes and known dependency vulnerabilities. They do not guarantee that dependencies are free of undiscovered vulnerabilities or that every operating-system configuration has been tested.

Applications deploying ETLRelay remain responsible for ongoing dependency maintenance and environment-specific security review.

docs.title: Current limitations and deferred risks
docs.text:
ETLRelay v1.0.0 does not provide:

  • Operating-system-level filesystem sandboxing or elimination of path-validation races.
  • A mechanism for safely executing arbitrary untrusted SQL or Python components.
  • A credential vault, credential rotation, or infrastructure access-control management.
  • Automatic sanitization of all third-party diagnostics.
  • Atomic file replacement or automatic recovery of previous output.
  • A transaction spanning multiple SQL batches or an entire pipeline.
  • Automatic retries, distributed transactions, or idempotency guarantees.
  • SQL schema migrations, table replacement, or upsert semantics.
  • A general-purpose remote-storage security model.
  • Comprehensive verification of all SQLAlchemy dialects and supported-platform combinations.

S3, HDFS, and other remote-storage implementations are outside the planned v1.0.0 scope. Additional integrations require their own security review and tests if introduced later.

These limitations should be evaluated explicitly when designing applications that use ETLRelay.

docs.title: Reporting vulnerabilities
docs.text:
Report suspected vulnerabilities privately using the repository's Security Policy.

Do not include real credentials, private datasets, or production records in reports. Parquet footer finalization follows primary-error precedence: a processing or serialization failure is preserved when finalization also fails, and the secondary warning identifies only the exception type. Failed finalization can leave unreadable partial output. This is not an atomic-write guarantee.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
ETLRelay uses explicit registries to associate each supported configuration type with both its configuration validator and runtime factory. The validator and PipelineBuilder consume the same registrations, reducing the risk that a type is accepted during validation but unavailable during construction.

The registry supports explicit application composition; it is not an automatic discovery or dynamic-plugin system. The default catalog defines a small fixed set of built-in components.

docs.title: Supported families
docs.text:
Family Registered names Registry Sources file, sql ComponentRegistry[Source] Sinks file, sql ComponentRegistry[Sink] Storage local ComponentRegistry[FileSystem] Processors select_columns, rename_columns, filter_rows ComponentRegistry[Processor] Tabular formats csv, parquet TabularFileFormatRegistry, with independent read/write capabilities Configuration document formats yaml KeyValueReader implementation; not part of the tabular format registry

Tabular formats are separate because a format can support reading, writing, or both. The format registry exposes capability queries without constructing readers/writers. YAML reads a mapping-shaped configuration document, not a stream of tabular Batch objects.

docs.title: Registration and dispatch
docs.text:
A ComponentRegistration[T] associates a ComponentConfigValidator with the factory used to build a component of type T. A ComponentRegistry[T] holds the explicit names and registrations for one family. Its lookup operation returns a registration or raises the registry's documented lookup error; it does not invoke the registration's factory.

The common ComponentConfigDispatcher checks mapping shape and the component type, then delegates validation through the matching registration. SourceConfigValidator, SinkConfigValidator, StorageConfigValidator, and ProcessorConfigValidator specialize this shared dispatch behavior with the appropriate registry and component-kind label. ProcessorSequenceConfigValidator validates the ordered list and delegates each element to the processor dispatcher with an indexed path.

Component-specific validators own their own property schema. The dispatcher does not contain file, sql, local, or processor-specific fields and never constructs runtime components.

docs.title: Default composition root
docs.text:
create_default_component_catalog() in etlrelay.default_components creates the shared registrations and services. It wires them in dependency order:

  1. Create the TabularFileFormatRegistry with CSV and Parquet readers and writers.
  2. Create the local storage registry and storage dispatcher.
  3. Create source and sink registrations that share the same storage and format registries where applicable.
  4. Create processor registrations pairing SelectColumns, RenameColumns, and FilterRows validators with their factories.
  5. Create source, sink, processor, and processor-sequence dispatchers.
  6. Create the root ConfigValidator and expose the shared objects through ComponentCatalog.

The caller may inject a SqlEngineFactory; otherwise the catalog creates one. The same SQL engine factory is injected into the built-in SQL source and sink factories and is exposed through the catalog for the builder's resource lifecycle.

Catalog creation instantiates registrations, validator objects, and factory objects. It does not call component factory build() methods, resolve SQL environment variables, create database engines, open data resources, or execute a pipeline.

docs.title: Pipeline construction
docs.text:
PipelineBuilder receives the source, sink, and processor registries from the same catalog. It resolves all registrations before SQL environment preflight or component construction. The order is deliberate: a configuration with an unknown component type or missing SQL URL must fail before any ETL component factory runs.

After all registrations and SQL references pass preflight, the builder constructs the source, processors in YAML order, and sink. It returns a Pipeline without executing it. If construction fails after SQL engines have been acquired during that attempt, the builder attempts to close the shared factory while preserving the original construction exception. On successful execution, the caller explicitly calls builder.close() to dispose the engines owned by the shared factory.

docs.title: Extension policy
docs.text:
Adding support for a component requires a runtime implementation, its component-specific configuration validator and factory, and one explicit registration in the default composition. It should not require changes to the generic registry, common dispatcher, unrelated validators, or ConfigValidator root rules, provided the root schema and supported component contract remain the same.

No automatic discovery, import-by-string, reflection-based construction, arbitrary user code execution, or mutable global service locator is provided in the frozen v1.0 scope. Applications can assemble their own explicit registries in Python. The default CLI catalog remains limited to the built-in types; custom registration does not automatically extend it.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
ETLRelay separates configuration-document parsing, schema validation, component construction, and pipeline execution.

ConfigLoader and ConfigValidator establish the configuration contract. PipelineBuilder resolves explicit component registrations, preflights required SQL environment-variable references, and constructs runtime components.

The pipeline executes only when the caller invokes Pipeline.run().

These responsibilities are shared by the direct Python APIs and the etlrelay CLI. Schema version 1 remains the supported configuration format in ETLRelay.

docs.title: End-to-end boundary
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    A[ConfigLoader.load path] --> B[FileSystem opens YAML file]
    B --> C[KeyValueReader.read stream]
    C --> D[YamlReader returns root mapping]
    D --> E[ConfigValidator.validate]
    E -->|valid mapping| F[PipelineBuilder.build]
    E -->|invalid schema| X[ConfigurationError]
    F --> G[Resolve all source, processor, and sink registrations]
    G --> H[SQL environment preflight]
    H -->|missing or empty reference| Y[PipelineBuildError]
    H --> I[Invoke component factories]
    I --> J[Return Pipeline]
    J --> K[Caller runs Pipeline.run]
    K --> L[Caller closes PipelineBuilder]

The configuration document itself has to be read. The no-side-effects guarantee concerns the configured ETL pipeline: schema validation does not open source/sink data files, connect to a database, create SQLAlchemy engines, invoke ETL component factories, or execute a pipeline. SQL URL environment variables are resolved during builder preflight; engines are created lazily when SQL component factories request them after successful preflight.

docs.title: KeyValueReader and YamlReader
docs.text:
KeyValueReader is a format-independent protocol for reading one mapping-shaped document from a binary stream. It is distinct from the tabular TabularReader protocol, which produces an iterable of ETLRelay Batch objects.

YamlReader lives in etlrelay.readers.yaml. It uses a safe PyYAML loader, rejects duplicate mapping keys (including duplicates after merge-key flattening), requires one document whose root is a mapping, and requires string keys at the root. It does not know ETLRelay's allowed configuration fields and does not perform application-schema validation. YamlReader leaves the supplied stream lifecycle to its caller.

docs.title: ConfigLoader
docs.text:
ConfigLoader receives a FileSystem, a KeyValueReader, and a ConfigValidator. load(path) opens the configuration resource through the injected filesystem, passes the stream to the reader within a context manager, validates the parsed object, and returns the mapping on success. It does not select a reader by file extension, construct components, resolve SQL variables, create engines, build a pipeline, or execute it.

ConfigLoader does not broadly translate exceptions. YAML parsing errors and filesystem errors propagate in their own exception types; schema validation failures are reported by ConfigurationError.

docs.title: ConfigValidator
docs.text:
ConfigValidator checks root-level properties and schema version 1, then delegates to the source, processor-sequence, and sink validators. Root values must be mappings with string keys. The root keys must be exactly version, source, processors, and sink, all required. The integer version check explicitly rejects YAML Boolean true.

Leaf and family validators return path-qualified error strings. ConfigValidator.validate() raises ConfigurationError when the root checks or any delegated validation produces errors; on success it returns None. The parsed mapping is returned by ConfigLoader.load(), not by the validator.

docs.title: PipelineBuilder
docs.text:
PipelineBuilder consumes validated configuration. It first resolves all source, sink, and processor registrations; then it collects SQL environment-variable references from configured SQL sources/sinks and performs preflight. It invokes component factories only after those steps succeed. Processors are constructed in YAML order.

The builder returns a Pipeline but does not execute it. With the default catalog, SQL source and sink factories share the catalog's SqlEngineFactory. Once the pipeline finishes, the caller calls builder.close() to dispose factory-owned engines and discard resolved URLs. Direct Python SqlSource/SqlSink usage retains the direct API's caller-owned engine lifecycle.

If component construction fails after SQL engines have been created in that build attempt, the builder attempts cleanup and preserves the original construction exception. A successful build must not close SQL resources before pipeline execution.

docs.title: Why parsing and validation are separate
docs.text:
A mapping document format reader knows YAML syntax, duplicate keys, document count, and root shape. The validator knows the ETLRelay schema—allowed component types, property names, property types, required fields, and schema version. Keeping these responsibilities separate permits a future mapping reader (such as JSON) without making it responsible for ETLRelay component names.

A future document format does not need to be part of the tabular TabularFileFormatRegistry. That registry is specifically about the ability to read and/or write tabular batches in CSV, Parquet, or another future tabular format.

docs.title: Error boundaries
docs.text: Boundary Examples Error behavior YAML parsing / shape Malformed YAML, duplicate mapping keys, multiple documents yaml.YAMLError, or YamlDocumentError (a ValueError subclass) for root-shape violations. Root and component schema Unsupported version, missing/unknown fields, invalid field types ConfigurationError raised by ConfigValidator. Build and preflight Unsupported/unregistered types, missing or empty SQL environment variables PipelineBuildError. Runtime execution File, query, schema, processor, or sink failures Underlying runtime exceptions propagate unless a component contract explicitly translates them.

docs.title: Scope
docs.text:
The supported configuration workflow includes YAML loading, schema validation, explicit component registration, SQL connection-reference preflight, runtime pipeline construction, and execution through the Python API or CLI.

The implementation does not support arbitrary dynamic imports, unrestricted Python expression evaluation, automatic plugin discovery, configuration inheritance, templating, or JSON configuration loading.

The configuration schema does not provide scheduling, distributed execution, or a general-purpose extension system.

Preflight guarantees apply to registration resolution and the required SQL environment-variable references. They do not establish runtime filesystem availability, database connectivity, SQL authorization, input-data compatibility, or successful output persistence.

For CLI behavior and exit codes, see the CLI Reference.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
ETLRelay validates schema-version-1 configuration before runtime components are constructed.

Validation uses explicit component registrations and component-specific validators. It does not use dynamic component discovery, arbitrary Python imports, or Python expression evaluation.

ETLRelay retains the version-1 configuration schema while strengthening SQL connection-reference validation and documenting the limits of configuration preflight.

See YAML Configuration for the supported component and property contract.

docs.title: Root schema validator
docs.text:
ConfigValidator accepts an object so it can defensively validate calls made outside the usual loader. It requires a mapping with string keys, rejects unknown top-level fields, requires version, source, processors, and sink, and requires the actual integer 1 for version—a Boolean is not accepted even though bool is an int subclass in Python.

When the root object cannot safely be interpreted as a string-keyed mapping, the validator raises ConfigurationError before delegating to section validators. Otherwise it checks root fields and delegates each present section to the injected source, processor-sequence, and sink validators. Errors are aggregated into one ConfigurationError rather than raising for each ordinary invalid property.

docs.title: Validator contract
docs.text:
ComponentConfigValidator is a Protocol exposing validate(config: object, path: str) -> list[str]. Concrete component validators return path-qualified error strings. An empty list indicates that no validation errors were found; a normal schema failure is not represented by an exception at the leaf-validator level.

This shared protocol applies to source/sink/storage dispatch and individual processors. The processor-sequence validator uses the same protocol to validate each list element.

docs.title: Dispatch and leaf validators
docs.text:
ComponentConfigDispatcher is the common dispatcher used by SourceConfigValidator, SinkConfigValidator, StorageConfigValidator, and ProcessorConfigValidator. It validates that the component configuration is a mapping with string keys, checks that type is a non-empty string, looks up the registration in its registry, and delegates to the registered validator. Invalid or unregistered types return path-specific validation messages. Validation does not invoke component factories.

Leaf validators own their own property rules:

  • File source: required path, format, and nested storage; the format registry must support reading.
  • File sink: required path, format, and nested storage; the format registry must support writing.
  • SQL source: connection_url_env must be a valid environment-variable identifier; query must be a nonempty string. Optional parameters must map string keys to supported scalar values or None.
  • SQL sink: connection_url_env must be a valid environment-variable identifier; table_name must be a nonempty string. Optional schema must be a nonempty string.
  • Local storage: type: local; optional base_path must be a non-empty string when present.
  • select_columns: required list of unique strings.
  • rename_columns: required mapping with string keys and values; data-dependent source/final-name constraints remain at processing time.
  • filter_rows: required non-empty column name, one of six supported comparison operators, and a string/integer/float/Boolean value (no null).

File source/sink validators share the storage validator and tabular file-format registry. They do not open data files. Format validation checks registry capabilities without constructing readers or writers.

docs.title: Processor sequence validation
docs.text: ProcessorSequenceConfigValidator requires a list and accepts an empty list. It visits each element in order and delegates to the processor dispatcher using paths such as processors[0] and processors[1]. Errors from an invalid element do not stop later elements from being validated. A missing root processors property is a root-level error; it is not equivalent to an empty list.

docs.title: Schema validation versus runtime validation
docs.text:
Configuration validation can check that a column list contains unique strings, but it cannot establish whether the source data contains those column names. It can check that a SQL query string and scalar parameters have supported types, but it does not execute the query. It can check a table-name string, but it does not connect to a database or verify that the destination table exists. Similarly, local path syntax/containment validation does not prove that the data file exists or is accessible.

Environment-variable names are part of the configuration and can be checked for shape during schema validation. Whether a connection-variable name resolves to a non-empty value is checked by PipelineBuilder's SQL preflight, before component factory construction and source/sink I/O.

The SQL configuration validators check the syntax of connection_url_env, not the contents of the referenced environment variable.

PipelineBuilder checks required variable presence and nonempty values during preflight before invoking component factories.

Neither stage guarantees that the resolved connection URL is valid, that a database can be reached, or that the database account has permission to execute the configured operations.

Actual query execution, destination column compatibility, and database constraints remain runtime responsibilities.

docs.title: Representative errors
docs.text:
Invalid configuration Example diagnostic Unsupported version version must be the integer 1. Unknown field source.fomrat is not a supported field. Missing discriminator source.type is required. Unsupported format sink.format 'xlsx' is not supported for writing. Invalid processor operator processors[0].operator must be one of '==', '!=', '<', '<=', '>', '>='.

Component validators aggregate ordinary validation errors as lists. ConfigValidator raises ConfigurationError with collected errors. Exact exception rendering depends on the exception's implemented string representation; the messages above illustrate the underlying validation diagnostics.

docs.title: Test responsibilities
docs.text:
• Leaf-validator unit tests use plain values and do not open files or connect to databases.
  • Dispatcher tests use fake/mocked registrations and assert the correct validator receives the original configuration and exact path.
  • Processor-sequence tests cover empty lists, non-lists, ordered indexed paths, and aggregation across multiple invalid entries.
  • Root-validator tests cover string-keyed mappings, required/unknown fields, strict integer version handling, delegation order, and aggregated errors.
  • Integration/functional tests exercise the actual default catalog and YAML loader; pipeline-builder tests separately verify preflight and no component construction on early failure.

See Configuration Loading Architecture and Component Registry Architecture.

docs.title: Status and scope
docs.text:
The tabular protocols are named TabularReader and TabularWriter. They read and write ETLRelay batches. KeyValueReader remains a separate protocol for reading mapping-shaped documents, with YamlReader as the existing implementation.

For v1.0, mapping-document writing and conversion between tabular batches and row records are deferred. Neither capability has a demonstrated requirement within the frozen feature set.

docs.title: Tabular batches
docs.text:
ETLRelay uses Batch objects, backed by PyArrow tables, as the common in-memory tabular representation. The current TabularReader protocol reads a binary stream and returns an iterable of batches; TabularWriter serializes an iterable of batches to a binary stream.

from collections.abc import Iterable
from typing import BinaryIO, Protocol

from etlrelay.core import Batch


class TabularReader(Protocol):
    def read(self, stream: BinaryIO) -> Iterable[Batch]:
        ...


class TabularWriter(Protocol):
    def write(self, batches: Iterable[Batch], stream: BinaryIO) -> None:
        ...

docs.title: Mapping-shaped documents
docs.text:
KeyValueReader reads one document mapping from a binary stream. YamlReader is the current implementation, using a safe loader and checking that the document root is a mapping with string keys. It rejects duplicate keys and multiple documents. It does not know the application schema.

from collections.abc import Mapping
from typing import Any, BinaryIO, Protocol


class KeyValueReader(Protocol):
    def read(self, stream: BinaryIO) -> Mapping[str, Any]:
        ...

ConfigLoader depends on KeyValueReader, not directly on YamlReader. ConfigValidator then applies the ETLRelay versioned schema, while PipelineBuilder consumes the validated configuration and constructs runtime components. The YAML reader never produces Batch objects and is not part of the tabular format registry.

docs.title: Row records
docs.text: A row record is an in-memory mapping such as {"id": 1, "name": "Ada"}. A sequence of such mappings is different from one configuration mapping and from an iterable of Batch objects. ETLRelay does not introduce a general conversion framework between these representations in the frozen v1.0 scope.

docs.title: Configuration loading boundary
docs.text:
Config file
    │
    ▼
FileSystem.open_read(path)
    │
    ▼
Binary stream
    │
    ▼
KeyValueReader.read(stream)  ──> one root Mapping[str, Any]
    │
    ▼
ConfigValidator.validate(mapping)
    │
    ▼
Validated mapping
    │
    ▼
PipelineBuilder.build(mapping)  ──> Pipeline

The loader must not construct sources, processors, sinks, SQLAlchemy engines, or pipelines. The builder owns component construction and SQL environment preflight. Schema validation and preflight occur before configured source/sink I/O starts.

docs.title: Format registry boundaries
docs.text:
TabularFileFormatRegistry contains reader and writer factories for tabular formats such as CSV and Parquet. It models reading and writing independently, because a format can be read-only or write-only. The default catalog registers CSV and Parquet readers/writers.

YamlReader is not a tabular format reader. It implements KeyValueReader and does not belong in the tabular registry. A future JsonReader could satisfy the same document-reader contract without changing the configuration schema, but JSON support is not included in the frozen v1.0 scope.

docs.title: Tabular/record conversion — deferred
docs.text: Tabular-to-records and records-to-tabular conversion are not required for v1.0. No conversion protocol or generic conversion framework is introduced. Before revisiting this decision, define a concrete consumer, eager/lazy row iteration, schema inference versus explicit schema, column order, missing/extra fields, empty input, null and Arrow-specific values, batching, and cleanup. Mapping-document parsing does not establish those row-conversion semantics.

docs.title: Protocol naming and mapping-document writing
docs.text:
TabularReader and TabularWriter explicitly identify the batch-oriented contracts. Concrete format implementations retain their existing names: CsvReader, ParquetReader, CsvWriter, and ParquetWriter.

KeyValueReader remains separate because one mapping-shaped document is a different representation from tabular batches or an iterable of row records.

KeyValueWriter is deferred beyond v1.0. Configuration loading requires document reading, and no mapping-document serialization use case currently justifies a writer protocol.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
FileSink is a sink component responsible for writing ETLRelay batches to a configured file resource.

It composes two independent components:

  • FileSystem, which provides a writable binary stream for the destination.
  • TabularWriter, which serializes an iterable of Batch objects into the supplied stream.

FileSink does not depend on a particular storage implementation or file format. The current implementation combines LocalFileSystem with CsvWriter or ParquetWriter without changing the sink implementation.

docs.title: FileSink
docs.text:
FileSink is responsible for:

  • Storing the configured destination path.
  • Opening the destination through the supplied FileSystem.
  • Passing the iterable of batches and writable stream to the supplied TabularWriter.
  • Opening the destination once per write operation rather than once per batch.
  • Ensuring the stream is closed after writing, including when serialization fails.
  • Implementing the Sink protocol.

FileSink is not responsible for:

  • Implementing filesystem operations.
  • Validating local filesystem path containment.
  • Serializing CSV, Parquet, or other file formats.
  • Transforming or constructing Batch objects.
  • Selecting a storage backend or writer implementation.
  • Orchestrating pipeline execution.
  • Defining format-specific behavior for empty batches.
  • Implementing application-level logging.

docs.title: FileSystem
docs.text:
FileSystem defines the storage contract used to open the destination for writing.

Its implementations handle storage-specific behavior, including resource access, opening writable streams, and any applicable path validation.

FileSink depends on the protocol rather than directly on LocalFileSystem.

docs.title: TabularWriter
docs.text:
TabularWriter defines the contract for serializing an iterable of Batch objects into a binary stream.

Its implementations handle format-specific serialization. The current built-in writers are CsvWriter and ParquetWriter.

The writer is responsible for processing the iterable according to its contract, including handling empty batches and determining how multiple batches are represented in one output resource. Format-specific constraints remain the writer's responsibility; for example, ParquetWriter requires a first batch to establish the output schema, so an empty iterable is not equivalent to a zero-row batch with a schema.

FileSink does not need to know how the writer serializes the batches.

Current file-based combinations use local storage with one of the built-in formats:

LocalFileSystem + ParquetWriter

Remote storage backends such as S3 and HDFS are not implemented in the frozen v1.0 scope and are not part of the planned v1.0.0 scope. Additional storage implementations may be reviewed after v1.0.0 if concrete requirements justify them; no particular backend or release date is promised.

docs.title: Data Flow
docs.text:
The sink coordinates the following operations:

FileSink.write(batches)
          │
          ▼
FileSystem.open_write(path)
          │
          ▼
    BinaryIO stream
          │
          ▼
TabularWriter.write(batches, stream)
          │
          ▼
   Serialized file data
          │
          ▼
       filesystem

The storage implementation provides the writable stream. The writer serializes the iterable of batches into that stream.

The stream is managed using a context manager so that it is closed after writing, including when serialization raises an exception.

A single call to FileSink.write() represents one output operation for the configured destination. All batches supplied in that call are handled by the writer through the same stream.

The sink does not buffer the entire iterable or independently iterate over it before passing it to the writer.

class FileSink:

        self,
        path: str,
        storage: FileSystem,
        writer: TabularWriter,

        ...

docs.title: Contract
docs.text:
Operation Expected behavior Construct with path, storage, and writer Stores the supplied dependencies and destination path Write an iterable of batches Delegates serialization to the supplied writer Write multiple batches Passes all batches through a single output stream Write an empty iterable Delegates empty-input handling to the writer Write an iterable containing empty batches Delegates empty-batch handling to the writer Write to a new valid local destination Creates the destination file when the parent directory exists and access is permitted Write to an invalid local path Propagates the path-validation error from local storage Write when storage access fails Propagates the underlying storage error Write when serialization fails Propagates the writer's exception Complete or fail a write Closes the opened stream Supply another storage implementation Works without modifying FileSink, provided it satisfies FileSystem and its behavioral contract Supply another writer implementation Works without modifying FileSink, provided it satisfies TabularWriter and its behavioral contract

Exceptions are propagated rather than wrapped in a new FileSink exception hierarchy.

For the current local filesystem implementation, opening a destination for writing uses binary write mode. An existing destination is therefore truncated, while a new destination is created if its parent directory exists and filesystem access is permitted. Parent directories are not created automatically.

FileSink closes the stream returned by FileSystem.open_write() on successful completion and on serialization failure.

With LocalFileSystem, opening an existing output truncates it immediately. A failure may leave an empty or partially written file; the previous contents are not restored.

FileSink does not provide atomic replacement or rollback. It delegates empty-input behavior to its configured writer.

docs.title: Single Responsibility Principle
docs.text:
FileSink has one primary responsibility: coordinating storage access and serialization to deliver batches to a file resource.

It does not implement filesystem operations or format-specific serialization.

docs.title: Open/Closed Principle
docs.text:
New writer implementations can be introduced without modifying FileSink. New storage implementations could also satisfy the protocol, but none beyond LocalFileSystem is currently included in the supported project scope.

For example, adding a new local-compatible writer does not require changes to the sink implementation.

No factory, registry, or plugin framework is required at this layer.

docs.title: Liskov Substitution Principle
docs.text: Any implementation satisfying FileSystem can be supplied as storage, and any implementation satisfying TabularWriter can be supplied as a writer, provided it preserves the documented behavioral contracts, including writable-stream behavior, iterable consumption, and exception propagation.

docs.title: Interface Segregation Principle
docs.text:
FileSink depends on two small protocols:

  • FileSystem provides writable resource access.
  • TabularWriter provides format-specific serialization.

Neither protocol needs unrelated operations such as pipeline orchestration or data transformation.

docs.title: Dependency Inversion Principle
docs.text:
FileSink depends on protocols rather than concrete storage and writer classes.

This keeps sink orchestration independent of local filesystem details and particular file formats.

docs.title: Design Constraints
docs.text:
The implementation should remain small:

  • Accept a destination path, FileSystem, and TabularWriter.
  • Use FileSystem.open_write() to obtain the output stream.
  • Pass the iterable of batches and stream to TabularWriter.write().
  • Open the destination once per write operation.
  • Close the stream reliably.
  • Propagate underlying exceptions.
  • Avoid format detection, factories, registries, retries, and append-mode configuration until concrete requirements justify them.

The central design principle is:

FileSink coordinates serialization and storage; the writer handles the format and iterable of batches, while the storage implementation handles the destination.

FileSource is responsible for:

  • Storing the configured resource path.
  • Opening the resource through the supplied FileSystem.
  • Passing the resulting binary stream to the supplied TabularReader.
  • Exposing the reader's batches through the Source interface.
  • Ensuring the opened stream remains available while batches are being read.
  • Closing the stream when iteration finishes, fails, or is explicitly closed.

FileSource is not responsible for:

  • Implementing filesystem operations.
  • Validating local filesystem path containment.
  • Parsing CSV, Parquet, or other file formats.
  • Constructing Batch objects directly.
  • Transforming data.
  • Writing files.
  • Orchestrating pipeline execution.

docs.title: FileSystem
docs.text:
FileSystem defines the contract for accessing file resources.

Its implementations open resources for reading and provide binary streams. Storage-specific behavior, such as local path validation, remains within the concrete storage implementation.

FileSource depends on the protocol rather than on LocalFileSystem.

docs.title: TabularReader
docs.text:
TabularReader defines the contract for parsing a binary stream and producing an iterable of ETLRelay Batch objects.

Its implementations handle format-specific parsing. The current built-in readers are CsvReader and ParquetReader.

A reader may produce one or more batches. FileSource does not need to know how the reader divides its output into batches or how it interprets the underlying format. Format-specific constraints remain the reader's responsibility; for example, the Parquet reader requires a seekable binary stream.

docs.title: Data Flow
docs.text:
The source coordinates the following operations:

FileSource.read()

Iterable[Batch]

Pipeline

The reader determines how many batches are produced. FileSource exposes those batches through the Source interface without performing additional format conversion or transformation.

The stream must remain open while the reader's iterable is consumed. This is particularly important when a reader produces batches lazily. The stream should be managed with a context manager so that it is closed reliably when iteration completes or terminates with an exception.

docs.title: Contract
docs.text:
Operation Expected behavior Construct with path, storage, and reader Stores the supplied dependencies and resource path Read a valid resource Produces an iterable of parsed batches Read a nonexistent local file Propagates the storage error Read an invalid CSV or Parquet resource Propagates the reader's parsing error Read a resource outside the permitted local base Propagates the path-validation error from local storage Consume batches Keeps the opened stream available while the reader's iterable is consumed Finish or terminate iteration Closes the opened stream Supply another storage implementation Works without modifying FileSource, provided it satisfies FileSystem and its behavioral contract Supply another reader implementation Works without modifying FileSource, provided it satisfies TabularReader and its behavioral contract

Exceptions are propagated rather than wrapped in a new FileSource exception hierarchy.

When FileSource.read() is consumed directly, the caller must explicitly close the returned generator if iteration stops early and deterministic cleanup is required.

When the source is used by Pipeline, the pipeline closes the active source iterator on termination. This includes early sink termination and failures during processing or writing.

FileSource owns the stream it opens, but does not own the injected FileSystem or TabularReader instances.

docs.title: Single Responsibility Principle
docs.text:
FileSource has one primary responsibility: coordinating storage access and format reading to produce batches for the pipeline.

It does not implement filesystem operations or format-specific parsing.

docs.title: Open/Closed Principle
docs.text:
New reader implementations can be introduced without modifying FileSource. New storage implementations could also satisfy the protocol, but none beyond LocalFileSystem is currently included in the supported project scope.

For example, adding a new reader for another supported local file format does not require changes to the source implementation.

No factory, registry, or plugin framework is required for this behavior.

docs.title: Liskov Substitution Principle
docs.text: Any implementation satisfying FileSystem can be supplied as storage, and any implementation satisfying TabularReader can be supplied as a reader, provided it preserves the documented contracts, including binary-stream behavior, batch iteration, resource lifetime, and exception propagation.

docs.title: Interface Segregation Principle
docs.text:
FileSource depends on two small protocols:

  • FileSystem provides resource access.
  • TabularReader provides format parsing and batch production.

Neither protocol needs unrelated operations such as writing, transformation, or pipeline execution.

docs.title: Dependency Inversion Principle
docs.text:
FileSource depends on protocols rather than concrete storage and reader classes.

This keeps source orchestration independent of local filesystem details and specific file formats.

docs.title: Design Constraints
docs.text:
The implementation should remain small:

  • Accept a resource path, FileSystem, and TabularReader.
  • Use FileSystem.open_read() to obtain the stream.
  • Pass the stream to TabularReader.read().
  • Expose the resulting batches through the Source interface.
  • Keep the stream open for the duration of iteration.
  • Close the stream reliably, including when iteration fails.
  • Propagate underlying exceptions.
  • Avoid format detection, factories, registries, retries, and additional chunking abstractions until concrete requirements justify them.

The central design principle is:

FileSource coordinates resource access and batch production; the storage implementation handles the resource, and the reader handles the format.

docs.text:
FilterRows is a built-in implementation of the Processor contract. It filters a Batch using one comparison between a named column and a configured value. Comparisons and row filtering use Apache Arrow compute operations.

The processor provides a deliberately small predicate interface; it does not implement an expression language or custom casting system.

docs.title: Responsibilities and behavior
docs.text:
FilterRows stores one column name, one supported comparison operator, and one comparison value. It returns a new Batch containing rows that satisfy the predicate.

Supported operators are ==, !=, <, <=, >, and >=.

Scenario Behavior Unsupported operator Raises ValueError during initialization. Unknown or ambiguous column Raises ValueError when processing a batch. Incompatible comparison types Raises TypeError; no custom casting is performed. Comparison evaluates to null Excludes the row. No rows match Returns a zero-row batch with the original schema. Input has zero rows Returns a zero-row batch with the original schema. All rows match Retains all rows and the original schema. Processor reused for another batch Processes that batch independently; input-batch state is not retained.

FilterRows does not alter the input schema, select or rename columns, perform I/O, or coordinate pipeline execution. Cross-batch output-schema compatibility is enforced by Pipeline, not by an individual processor.

See Core Concepts for the batch model and API Reference for constructor details.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
FileSystem is a protocol defining the storage-access contract used by ETLRelay's file sources and sinks.

LocalFileSystem implements this protocol by providing readable and writable binary streams for local filesystem paths.

Storage access is separated from file-format handling. LocalFileSystem does not know about CSV, Parquet, Batch, readers, writers, sources, sinks, or pipeline orchestration.

For local filesystem security, LocalFileSystem uses PathValidator to ensure that paths resolve within the configured permitted directory.
