docs.title: FileSystem
docs.text:
FileSystem defines the minimal storage contract required by file sources and sinks.

It is responsible for exposing operations that open resources as binary streams:

  • open_read() opens a resource for reading.
  • open_write() opens a resource for writing.

FileSystem is not responsible for:

  • Parsing or serializing file formats.
  • Creating or interpreting Batch objects.
  • Implementing source or sink orchestration.
  • Pipeline execution.
  • Application-level logging.

The protocol is intentionally small so that multiple storage implementations can satisfy the same contract.

docs.title: LocalFileSystem
docs.text:
LocalFileSystem is responsible for:

  • Opening local files for binary reading.
  • Opening local files for binary writing.
  • Validating path containment through PathValidator.
  • Translating a FileNotFoundError raised while opening an input file into FileSystemError, including when the file disappears after path validation.
  • Returning binary streams to callers.
  • Propagating filesystem access errors.

LocalFileSystem is not responsible for:

  • Parsing CSV, Parquet, or other formats.
  • Serializing Batch objects.
  • Selecting readers or writers.
  • Creating missing parent directories.
  • Source or sink orchestration.
  • Pipeline execution.
  • Application-level logging.

The storage implementation handles filesystem existence and I/O behavior. PathValidator handles path containment.

docs.title: PathValidator
docs.text:
PathValidator determines whether a candidate path resolves within its configured base directory.

It accepts paths represented as Path objects or strings and returns the resolved path when the containment check succeeds.

It does not check whether the path exists.

This separation supports both input and output paths:

FileSource
    │
    └── Existing input path
            │
            ▼
       LocalFileSystem
            │
            ▼
         open_read()

FileSink
    │
    └── Existing or new output path
            │
            ▼
       LocalFileSystem
            │
            ▼
         open_write()

docs.title: Dependency Relationship
docs.text:
FileSource and FileSink depend on the FileSystem protocol rather than directly on LocalFileSystem.

FileSource ──┐
             ├──> FileSystem
FileSink ────┘
                  ▲
                  │ implements
                  │
             LocalFileSystem
                  │
                  ▼
             PathValidator

The current storage implementation is LocalFileSystem. S3, HDFS, and other remote-storage backends are not included in v0.4.0 or the planned v1.0.0 scope.

The FileSystem protocol establishes a small storage-access boundary, but it does not mean that remote backends are implemented or committed for a future release. Additional storage and platform integrations may be reviewed after v1.0.0 if concrete requirements justify them. No particular backend or release date is promised.

docs.title: FileSource
docs.text:
FileSource
    │
    ├── FileSystem.open_read(path)
    │          │
    │          ▼
    │       BinaryIO
    │          │
    │          ▼
    └────── TabularReader.read(stream)
                   │
                   ▼
             Iterable[Batch]

The storage component opens the resource, and the reader interprets its contents. The reader may produce multiple batches from one resource.

docs.title: FileSink
docs.text:
FileSink
    │
    ├── FileSystem.open_write(path)
    │          │
    │          ▼
    │       BinaryIO
    │          │
    │          ▼
    └────── TabularWriter.write(batches, stream)
                   │
                   ▼
              Serialized data

The writer serializes the supplied batches into the output stream. The storage component determines where the stream is stored.

FileSource and FileSink manage the streams they open.

FileSource.read() performs file access lazily, as its returned generator is consumed. The input stream is closed when iteration completes, reading raises an exception, or the generator is explicitly closed. Consumers that stop iterating early should explicitly close the generator when deterministic cleanup is required.

FileSink closes the output stream after writing succeeds or fails. Exceptions raised by the reader or writer propagate to the caller without being converted into generic source or sink exceptions.

Opening an output uses truncating write mode. If a writer fails, a partial or empty output file may remain; an existing destination may already have been truncated. The storage contract does not guarantee rollback or atomic replacement.

from typing import BinaryIO

from etlrelay.security import PathValidator


class LocalFileSystem:
    def __init__(self, path_validator: PathValidator) -> None:

    def open_read(self, path: str) -> BinaryIO:
        ...

    def open_write(self, path: str) -> BinaryIO:
        ...

docs.title: Contract
docs.text:
Operation Expected behavior open_read(path) Validates path containment and opens the file in binary read mode (rb). It does not perform a separate existence check before opening. open_write(path) Validates path containment and opens the file in binary write mode (wb). Open a nonexistent input file Translates FileNotFoundError from the open operation into FileSystemError. Open a new output with an existing parent directory Creates the destination file. Open an existing output Truncates its existing contents when the file is opened. Open an output whose parent directory is missing Propagates FileNotFoundError; parent directories are not created automatically. Access a path outside the permitted base Raises PathValidationError. Encounter another filesystem failure Propagates the original filesystem exception.

The behavior above describes LocalFileSystem. The FileSystem protocol defines the stream-opening interface; implementations must document and satisfy the behavioral contract expected by their consumers.

Both operations return binary streams owned by the caller. Direct callers must close returned streams. When the streams are used through FileSource or FileSink, those components manage their respective stream lifetimes.

PathValidator is responsible for path containment, not existence or access-permission checks. Filesystem operations determine whether a resource can be opened.

docs.title: Single Responsibility Principle
docs.text:
LocalFileSystem has one primary responsibility: providing local filesystem access.

Path containment is delegated to PathValidator, while parsing and serialization are delegated to readers and writers.

docs.title: Open/Closed Principle
docs.text:
Additional storage implementations can satisfy FileSystem without requiring modifications to FileSource or FileSink.

The current implementation does not require a storage factory, registry, or plugin mechanism.

docs.title: Liskov Substitution Principle
docs.text:
Any implementation satisfying FileSystem can be supplied to a file source or sink, provided it preserves the protocol's behavioral contract.

Implementations must return usable binary streams and document their storage-specific behavior consistently.

docs.title: Interface Segregation Principle
docs.text:
FileSystem exposes only two operations:

  • Opening a resource for reading.
  • Opening a resource for writing.

It does not expose unrelated filesystem administration operations such as directory traversal, permissions management, metadata management, or deletion.

docs.title: Dependency Inversion Principle
docs.text:
FileSource and FileSink depend on FileSystem, not on LocalFileSystem.

LocalFileSystem depends on PathValidator to enforce local path containment.

This keeps the higher-level components independent of local filesystem details.

docs.title: Design Constraints
docs.text:
The storage protocol operates on binary streams rather than requiring callers to read or write an entire resource as bytes.

This allows readers and writers to operate on streams without requiring the storage component to load the entire serialized resource into memory first.

Readers and writers operate on binary streams, so they do not need to know where the data is stored. The current implementation provides local filesystem access through LocalFileSystem. Additional implementations would require their own implementation and contract tests; none is included in the v0.4.0 milestone or planned v1.0.0 scope.

LocalFileSystem should continue using Python's standard filesystem APIs and pathlib.Path internally.

PathValidator remains responsible for local path containment. LocalFileSystem remains responsible for existence checks and filesystem operations.

No additional abstractions such as storage factories, registries, remote filesystem base classes, or generic resource managers are required at this stage.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
ETLRelay is organized around composable runtime contracts and a separate configuration-construction layer. Pipeline coordinates batch processing; sources obtain data, processors transform batches, and sinks consume the processed output. File sources and sinks compose filesystem access with format-specific readers and writers.

ETLRelay also permits users to declare supported pipelines in YAML. Configuration parsing, schema validation, component registration lookup, pipeline construction, and execution remain separate responsibilities.

docs.title: Runtime and configuration diagrams
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    subgraph Runtime pipeline
        S[Source] --> B[Iterable of Batch]
        B --> P[Processors in declared order]
        P --> K[Sink]
    end
    subgraph Configuration path
        Y[YAML document] --> L[ConfigLoader / YamlReader]
        L --> V[ConfigValidator]
        V --> M[Validated mapping]
        M --> C[ComponentCatalog registrations]
        C --> PB[PipelineBuilder]
        PB --> S
        PB --> K
        PB --> P
    end

The configuration loader and validator do not construct runtime components. PipelineBuilder resolves all component registrations and preflights SQL environment references before it invokes component factories. It returns a Pipeline; the caller separately executes pipeline.run().

docs.title: Component responsibilities
docs.text: Component Responsibility Batch Wraps the Arrow table used as the pipeline's common tabular representation. Source Produces an iterable of batches. Processor Transforms one batch through process(batch: Batch) -> Batch. Sink Consumes an iterable of processed batches. Pipeline Applies processors in order and validates processed output schemas during a run. FileSource / FileSink Compose storage access with reading or writing. FileSystem Opens readable or writable binary streams. TabularReader / TabularWriter Convert between serialized tabular formats and batches. KeyValueReader / YamlReader Parse one mapping-shaped configuration document; does not produce batches. ConfigLoader Coordinates configuration-file reading, parsing, and validation. ConfigValidator Validates version 1 of the YAML configuration schema. ComponentRegistry Maps explicitly supported component names to validator/factory registrations. ComponentCatalog Shares default registries, validators, factories, and SQL engine service. PipelineBuilder Resolves registrations, preflights SQL environment variables, and builds a runtime pipeline.

docs.title: File runtime path
docs.text:
FileSystem.open_read(path)
          │
          ▼
      BinaryIO stream
          │
          ▼
       TabularReader.read(stream)
          │
          ▼
        Iterable[Batch]

The write path operates in the reverse direction. LocalFileSystem and PathValidator handle local resource access and path containment. CSV and Parquet formats are registered separately with independent reader/writer capabilities.

docs.title: Configuration path
docs.text:
ConfigLoader accepts a FileSystem, KeyValueReader, and ConfigValidator. Its load(path) method opens and parses the configuration document, closes the stream, validates the mapping, and returns that mapping. YAML syntax/root-shape failures, filesystem errors, and schema validation errors keep their distinct error boundaries.

ConfigValidator checks the root schema and delegates to source, processor-sequence, and sink validators. Dispatchers look up explicit ComponentRegistration instances and delegate to their configuration validators; factories are not called during validation.

create_default_component_catalog() wires a shared tabular-format registry, storage/source/sink/processor registries, dispatchers, root validator, and SQL engine factory. PipelineBuilder uses the same registries. This is an explicit composition root for a fixed built-in component set, not a dynamic plugin system.

docs.title: SQL ownership
docs.text: Direct Python SqlSource and SqlSink components borrow the SQLAlchemy engine supplied by the caller. Configuration-built pipelines share the catalog's SqlEngineFactory, which resolves environment-variable references before engine creation and caches engines on demand. The caller must close the PipelineBuilder after execution so the factory disposes of the engines it owns.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
PathValidator is a security component responsible for ensuring that a filesystem path resolves within an explicitly permitted base directory.

It resolves candidate paths before checking containment, preventing relative path traversal and symlink-based paths from escaping the permitted boundary.

PathValidator is intentionally small and independent of ETLRelay's storage, source, sink, reader, and writer implementations. LocalFileSystem uses it to validate local filesystem paths before performing I/O.

Path validation does not require the candidate to exist. Filesystem existence and access errors are handled by the storage component.

docs.title: PathValidator
docs.text:
PathValidator is responsible for:

  • Accepting an optional base directory during construction.
  • Defaulting the base directory to the current working directory when none is provided.
  • Resolving the base directory and candidate paths.
  • Determining whether a resolved candidate remains within the permitted base directory.
  • Returning the resolved path when valid.
  • Raising PathValidationError when a candidate escapes the permitted boundary.

PathValidator is not responsible for:

  • Checking whether a candidate path exists.
  • Opening, reading, or writing files.
  • Creating directories.
  • Parsing CSV or other data formats.
  • Knowing about Batch.
  • Knowing about Source, Sink, or pipeline execution.
  • Performing authorization or user-level access control.
  • Logging application-level events.

docs.title: Dependency Relationship
docs.text:
LocalFileSystem
       │
       ▼
PathValidator

LocalFileSystem depends on PathValidator to enforce local path containment before performing filesystem operations.

PathValidator does not depend on LocalFileSystem or any higher-level ETLRelay component. It uses Python's pathlib.Path for path resolution and containment checks.

FileSource and FileSink depend on the FileSystem protocol rather than on PathValidator directly. Path validation is handled by the concrete local storage implementation.

docs.title: Interface
docs.text:
from pathlib import Path


class PathValidator:
    def __init__(self, base_path: Path | None = None) -> None:
        ...

    def validate(self, path: Path | str) -> Path:
        ...


class PathValidationError(Exception):
    """Raised when a filesystem path fails validation."""

docs.title: Contract
docs.text: Operation Expected behavior Construct without a base path Uses the resolved current working directory Construct with an explicit base path Uses the resolved supplied directory as the permitted boundary Validate a contained relative path Returns the resolved path Validate a contained absolute path Returns the resolved path Validate the base directory itself Returns the resolved base path Validate a path containing safe . or .. segments Returns the resolved path if it remains within the boundary Validate a path containing traversal that escapes the base Raises PathValidationError Validate an absolute path outside the base Raises PathValidationError Validate a path with a similar directory-name prefix outside the base Raises PathValidationError Validate a symlink resolving inside the base Returns the resolved target path Validate a symlink resolving outside the base Raises PathValidationError Validate a nonexistent path inside the base Returns the resolved path; existence is not checked

docs.title: Single Responsibility Principle
docs.text:
PathValidator has one reason to change: the rules governing local filesystem path containment.

It does not combine path validation with filesystem I/O, data-format handling, or application logic.

docs.title: Open/Closed Principle
docs.text:
The implementation remains deliberately small. Additional path policies should be introduced only when concrete requirements justify them.

No path-policy hierarchy or configurable validation framework is required.

docs.title: Liskov Substitution Principle
docs.text: No inheritance hierarchy is required. PathValidator is a concrete security utility whose behavior is defined by its contract.

docs.title: Interface Segregation Principle
docs.text: No protocol is necessary for the current implementation. PathValidator exposes only the operation its consumer requires: validate().

docs.title: Dependency Inversion Principle
docs.text:
LocalFileSystem delegates path-containment checks to PathValidator rather than implementing its own validation logic.

PathValidator depends only on Python's standard path-handling functionality and remains independent of higher-level ETLRelay components.

docs.title: Design Constraints
docs.text:
The implementation should use pathlib.Path and explicit path containment rather than string-prefix comparisons.

The validator establishes its permitted boundary during construction:

PathValidator(base_path)
        │
        ▼
  trusted boundary
        │
        ▼
validate(candidate_path)
        │
        ├── contained ──> resolved Path
        │
        └── outside ────> PathValidationError

The containment check must occur after path resolution so that traversal segments and symlinks are evaluated against their resolved locations.

Path existence is deliberately outside this component's contract:

PathValidator
      │
      ├── contained path ──> resolved Path
      │
      └── escaping path ───> reject

LocalFileSystem
      │
      ├── open existing resource for reading
      │
      └── open destination for writing

PathValidator establishes a path-containment boundary; it is not a complete filesystem sandbox or authorization mechanism. Filesystem changes between validation and subsequent use can still create time-of-check-to-time-of-use risks.

No additional abstractions such as PathPolicy, PathResolver, or a filesystem interface are required for this component.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: Pipeline coordinates a source, an ordered sequence of processors, and a sink. It executes synchronously, processes batches in source order, applies processors in their configured order, and passes processed output to the sink.

docs.title: Execution flow
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    A[Source.read] --> B{Another batch?}
    B -->|yes| C[First processor]
    C --> D[Next processor, in order]
    D --> E[Validate processed output schema]
    E --> F[Yield batch to sink]
    F --> B
    B -->|no| G[Finish]

The pipeline does not buffer all source batches before writing. A failure while reading, processing, validating, or writing propagates to the caller. Previously written batches are not automatically rolled back.

docs.title: Output schema compatibility
docs.text:
The first processed output batch establishes the expected output schema. Each subsequent processed batch must match its field names, field order, Arrow data types, and nullability. Schema metadata differences are ignored. Validation occurs after all processors have run, so processors can normalize input batches before the compatibility check.

An incompatible output batch causes ValueError before that batch is passed to the sink. The pipeline does not automatically merge schemas, cast values, or reconcile incompatible outputs.

docs.title: Empty data
docs.text:
A zero-row Batch retains its schema and is processed normally. It participates in output schema validation and is delivered to the sink if processing succeeds.

An empty source iterable has no batches: processors are not invoked and the sink is not invoked. This is distinct from one zero-row batch.

docs.title: Direct construction and YAML construction
docs.text:
The pipeline contract is the same whether constructed directly in Python or from YAML. YAML does not change the execution semantics of Pipeline; it changes how the runtime components are selected and composed.

For a YAML configuration, the application flow is:

  1. Load and validate the document with ConfigLoader and ConfigValidator.
  2. Call PipelineBuilder.build(validated_config) to resolve registered components, preflight SQL environment-variable references, and construct the runtime objects.
  3. Call pipeline.run() to execute the pipeline.
  4. Call builder.close() after execution to release SQLAlchemy engines owned by the shared SqlEngineFactory.

PipelineBuilder.build() does not call run(). The caller controls execution and resource cleanup. Direct Python SQL components retain their original engine ownership contract; they do not take ownership of the engine passed to their constructors.

docs.title: Error boundaries
docs.text:
Configuration-schema errors are raised by ConfigValidator as ConfigurationError. Component type/preflight/construction errors from PipelineBuilder use PipelineBuildError for builder-level failures, while exceptions from runtime sources, processors, and sinks propagate according to their component contracts. The builder does not wrap all pipeline execution errors.

See YAML Configuration, Configuration Loading Architecture, and Core Concepts.

docs.title: Resource lifecycle and failure semantics
docs.text: Pipeline coordinates execution and consumes batches lazily. It does not own the underlying storage backends, database engines, readers, writers, or component instances.

docs.title: Source iterator cleanup
docs.text:
During Pipeline.run(), ETLRelay consumes the iterable returned by Source.read() and passes processed batches to the configured sink.

When execution terminates, the pipeline attempts to close its processing iterator and the underlying source iterator if they expose callable close() methods.

Cleanup occurs when:

  • The sink consumes all batches successfully.
  • The source produces no batches.
  • The sink returns without consuming every batch.
  • The source or a processor raises an exception.
  • The sink raises an exception.
  • A later batch fails schema validation.

Closing an iterator allows a lazy source such as FileSource to release a stream that is still open because iteration stopped early.

The Source protocol returns Iterable[Batch] and does not require every iterable to support close(). The pipeline only invokes that method when available.

Direct consumers of FileSource.read() must explicitly close the generator when they stop iteration early and require deterministic resource cleanup.

docs.title: Failure and cleanup precedence
docs.text:
Exceptions from sources, processors, and sinks propagate to the caller.

If execution fails and iterator cleanup also fails, the execution error takes precedence. Secondary cleanup failures are reported through safe operational warnings.

If execution succeeds but iterator cleanup fails, the first cleanup exception propagates after cleanup has been attempted for the remaining iterators.

The pipeline does not log successful completion when required cleanup fails.

docs.title: Empty sources and zero-row batches
docs.text:
A source producing no batches causes the pipeline to finish without invoking the sink. No destination is opened by the sink in this case, and an existing output file is not truncated.

A source producing a zero-row batch is different. That batch is processed, schema-validated, and passed to the sink.

The first processed batch establishes the expected schema even when it contains no rows.

The concrete sink or writer determines what is persisted for a zero-row batch.

docs.title: Schema compatibility
docs.text:
Every processed output batch must match the schema established by the first processed output batch.

Compatibility requires matching:

  • Field names and order.
  • Arrow field types.
  • Field nullability.

Schema metadata differences are ignored.

This validation includes zero-row batches. A later incompatible batch raises ValueError before being delivered to the sink.

The pipeline does not attempt automatic type casting, field reordering, or schema reconciliation.

docs.title: Partial writes and rollback
docs.text:
The pipeline does not provide atomic execution or transaction rollback across an entire run.

A failure can occur after one or more earlier batches have already been written.

The resulting persistence behavior depends on the sink:

  • File sinks: Output streams close on completion or failure, but an empty or partially written destination may remain. Existing files may already have been truncated.
  • SQL sinks: Each nonempty batch uses its own transaction. The failed transaction is rolled back, while earlier successfully committed batches remain committed.

The pipeline does not retry failed operations or automatically restore previous output.

Applications requiring atomic replacement, pipeline-wide transactions, or idempotent retries must implement those guarantees outside the current ETLRelay contracts.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
ETLRelay uses separate contracts for tabular data and mapping-shaped documents. This distinction matters now that YAML configuration is supported: a tabular reader produces Batch objects, while a key-value reader produces one configuration document mapping.

The public tabular protocols are TabularReader and TabularWriter. The former Reader and Writer class names are removed without aliases. Their modules remain etlrelay.core.reader and etlrelay.core.writer; KeyValueReader remains in etlrelay.core.reader.

docs.title: Tabular TabularReader and TabularWriter
docs.text:
TabularReader consumes a binary stream and produces an iterable of Batch objects. TabularWriter consumes an iterable of batches and serializes them to a binary stream. The protocols separate format-specific parsing/serialization from storage access.

flowchart LR
    A[FileSystem.open_read] --> B[BinaryIO]
    B --> C[TabularReader.read]
    C --> D[Iterable of Batch]
    D --> E[Processor pipeline]
    E --> F[TabularWriter.write]
    F --> G[BinaryIO]
    G --> H[FileSystem.open_write]

FileSource composes a filesystem with a TabularReader; FileSink composes a filesystem with a TabularWriter. Readers and writers do not locate paths or validate filesystem containment. The component that opens a stream remains responsible for closing it.

Built-in tabular implementations:

Format TabularReader TabularWriter Notes CSV CsvReader CsvWriter Text format; Arrow types are inferred on reading, so exact schema round trips are not guaranteed. Parquet ParquetReader ParquetWriter Columnar format preserving supported Arrow schema/type information. The reader requires a seekable binary stream. The writer needs a first batch to establish schema; an empty iterable raises WriterError, while a zero-row batch with a schema is valid.

TabularFileFormatRegistry registers the reader and writer factories independently. File-source validation asks whether a format supports reading; file-sink validation asks whether it supports writing. Capability checks do not invoke factories.

docs.title: KeyValueReader and YamlReader
docs.text:
KeyValueReader is a separate protocol used for mapping-shaped documents. Its contract returns one root mapping with string keys; it does not return batches and is not substitutable for the tabular TabularReader protocol.

YamlReader implements KeyValueReader and lives in etlrelay.readers.yaml. It uses PyYAML's safe loader and owns document-format concerns:

  • Parses one YAML document from a binary stream.
  • Rejects duplicate mapping keys, including collisions after YAML merge-key flattening.
  • Rejects unhashable mapping keys and malformed YAML.
  • Requires the root value to be a mapping with string keys.
  • Leaves schema validation to ConfigValidator.
  • Leaves stream ownership to its caller.

The reader does not know the allowed ETLRelay schema fields or supported source, sink, processors, storage, and format types. It parses the document without creating components, resolving environment variables, accessing configured data resources, or running a pipeline.

docs.title: Configuration data flow
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    A[ConfigLoader.load path] --> B[FileSystem opens config file]
    B --> C[KeyValueReader.read]
    C --> D[YamlReader mapping]
    D --> E[ConfigValidator]
    E --> F[Validated mapping]
    F --> G[PipelineBuilder]

The configuration file is read through the filesystem abstraction just like other file resources, but configuration parsing is a distinct boundary. Validation and pipeline construction are described in Configuration Loading Architecture and Configuration Validation Architecture.

docs.title: What this interface does not do
docs.text:
Neither tabular TabularReader/TabularWriter nor KeyValueReader converts arbitrary row records to/from batches. A mapping-shaped document, a sequence of row mappings, and an iterable of Batch objects are different representations with different contracts. Generic tabular-to-record conversion is deferred beyond v1.0 and is not implied by YAML configuration support.

A future JSON document reader could implement KeyValueReader without changing ConfigLoader or the configuration schema validator. It would not need to join TabularFileFormatRegistry.

docs.title: Responsibilities and resource lifecycle
docs.text: Component Responsibility Does not own FileSystem Opens resource streams by path Format parsing or transformation TabularReader Parses a tabular stream into batches Opening/closing the stream or validating the path TabularWriter Serializes batches to a stream Opening/closing the stream or choosing destination paths KeyValueReader Reads one mapping-shaped document ETLRelay configuration schema validation YamlReader Safe YAML syntax and root mapping contract ETL component construction or execution ConfigValidator Schema version, fields, component types, and property constraints File/DB I/O or runtime component construction ConfigLoader Coordinates config-file reading and validation Building or running a pipeline

docs.title: Stream ownership
docs.text:
Readers and writers borrow streams supplied by their callers.

  • TabularReader.read(stream) must not close the supplied input stream.
  • TabularWriter.write(batches, stream) must not close the supplied output stream.
  • This ownership rule applies to successful operations and failures.
  • Direct callers must manage the streams they supply.
  • FileSource and FileSink manage the streams they obtain through their configured FileSystem.

Format-specific requirements remain the responsibility of each reader or writer. For example, Parquet reading requires an appropriately seekable binary stream.

Readers and writers do not create directories, open paths independently, or manage storage-backend lifetimes.

docs.title: Empty-input and schema behavior
docs.text:
Readers and writers implement format-specific serialization contracts. Consequently, empty inputs and schema compatibility may behave differently between CSV and Parquet.

Input CsvWriter ParquetWriter No batches Writes no bytes Raises WriterError One schema-bearing zero-row batch Writes the CSV header Writes a valid empty Parquet file Compatible batches with metadata differences Uses CSV field names and values without preserving Arrow metadata Accepts metadata-only differences Incompatible batch schemas Behavior depends on CSV writer validation and serialization requirements Raises WriterError

docs.title: CSV
docs.text:
CSV is a text-based format and does not preserve Arrow data types, field nullability, or schema metadata.

A zero-row batch with named columns produces a CSV header without data rows.

An entirely empty iterable produces no serialized content.

On input, a header-only CSV produces no batches. A zero-byte CSV file is invalid and raises pyarrow.ArrowInvalid; it is not treated as a successful empty source.

docs.title: Parquet
docs.text:
Parquet preserves structured schema information, including Arrow data types.

The first batch establishes the output schema. Subsequent batches must have compatible field names, order, types, and nullability.

Schema metadata differences are permitted, but the output uses the schema established by the first batch.

A schema-bearing zero-row batch produces a valid Parquet file containing no data rows.

An entirely empty iterable cannot establish an output schema and raises WriterError.

After batch serialization or upstream iteration fails, ParquetWriter still attempts to finalize its native writer. The original failure takes precedence if finalization also fails. A secondary finalization failure is logged using only its exception type. If serialization otherwise succeeds, a finalization failure propagates to the caller.

The supplied stream remains caller-owned on both paths. Successfully finalized partial output can contain earlier batches; if finalization fails, the output may be unreadable. Neither outcome constitutes a successful pipeline run or provides rollback.

docs.title: Pipeline validation
docs.text:
When readers and writers are used through Pipeline, the pipeline applies its own schema compatibility checks before yielding batches to the sink.

Zero-row batches participate in this validation, and schema metadata differences are ignored.

TabularWriter-specific serialization requirements remain in effect even when batches have passed pipeline validation.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: SelectColumns and RenameColumns are built-in implementations of the existing Processor contract. They transform the Apache Arrow table held by a Batch and return a new Batch. Neither processor performs I/O or coordinates pipeline execution.

docs.title: SelectColumns
docs.text:
SelectColumns selects the configured columns in the order supplied to its constructor. It preserves the selected columns' values, Arrow data types, and nullability.

It raises ValueError for duplicate requested names or requested names that are missing or ambiguous in the input batch. A zero-row table retains the selected schema.

docs.title: RenameColumns
docs.text:
RenameColumns renames columns using a mapping from existing names to new names. It preserves field order, values, data types, and nullability.

It raises ValueError if a source name is unknown or if the resulting column names would not be unique. Multiple columns can be renamed simultaneously, including swapping names, when all final names are unique.

docs.title: Composition
docs.text:
Both classes satisfy the same processor contract:

process(batch: Batch) -> Batch

They can be used independently or sequentially. For example, SelectColumns can first choose and order a subset of columns, after which RenameColumns changes the names of the selected fields. Their order matters because each processor receives the previous processor's output.

Neither processor depends on the other. Column selection and renaming do not read files, write output, filter rows, or perform automatic type conversions.

See Core Concepts for the batch model and API Reference for constructor details.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
SqlSource and SqlSink connect database I/O to ETLRelay's existing Source and Sink contracts. They are separate from FileSource, FileSink, the filesystem protocol, and file-format readers/writers. SQL components exchange the same Arrow-backed Batch representation used by the rest of the pipeline.

flowchart LR
    DB[(SQL database)] --> SqlSource[SqlSource]
    SqlSource --> Batch[Batch]
    Batch --> Pipeline["Processor(s) / Pipeline"]
    Pipeline --> SqlSink[SqlSink]
    SqlSink --> DB2[(SQL database table)]

A SQL engine is created and owned by the caller. ETLRelay borrows the engine to obtain connections and transactions; it does not dispose the caller's engine.

docs.title: Public API
docs.text:
SqlSource(
    engine,
    query,
    *,
    parameters=None,
)

SqlSink(
    engine,
    table_name,
    *,
    schema=None,
)

See the API Reference for the generated public signatures and parameter types.

docs.title: SqlSource
docs.text:
SqlSource executes a caller-provided SQL text query through SQLAlchemy. Optional parameters supplies a mapping of parameter names to values, bound through SQLAlchemy rather than interpolated into the query string.

For a query that returns rows, SqlSource.read() converts the result into one Batch. All rows are materialized before the connection is closed; the source is therefore batch-oriented, not a streaming or paginated database reader. A query returning no rows produces an empty iterable, not a zero-row batch. Duplicate result-column names are rejected because conversion through row mappings would otherwise make the result ambiguous. Arrow itself can represent duplicate field names.

Use named bind parameters for values:

source = SqlSource(
    engine,
    "SELECT id, amount FROM orders WHERE status = :status ORDER BY id",
    parameters={"status": "ready"},
)

Do not build value predicates using f-strings or string concatenation. Binding protects the value boundary; it does not bind SQL syntax such as a table name, column name, operator, or sort direction.

SqlSource closes its SQLAlchemy result after retrieving rows, including when result validation or iteration fails. Its connection is also released on success or failure.

Arrow conversion occurs after the query result has been materialized. The caller's engine remains open and is never disposed by SqlSource.

docs.title: SqlSink
docs.text:
SqlSink reflects a destination table that must already exist and inserts incoming rows into it. Its supported behavior is append only. It does not create a table, replace a table, update or upsert existing rows, delete rows, or migrate a schema.

The names supplied by table_name and optional schema are passed to SQLAlchemy's table-reflection/insert APIs. SQLAlchemy handles dialect-specific identifier quoting for those table operations. These values are identifiers, not query-value parameters. For identifiers that originate from outside the application, validate or allowlist them before constructing the component.

Each incoming batch must have unique column names, and every batch column must match a column in the reflected destination table. Unknown target columns and duplicate batch column names raise ValueError. Destination columns omitted from a batch must be nullable, have a database default, or otherwise be satisfied by the database; database constraint violations propagate from SQLAlchemy/the driver.

sink = SqlSink(engine, "processed_orders")
sink.write(batches)

The call above illustrates the API shape only; it assumes that processed_orders already exists and that each batch has compatible destination columns.

docs.title: Resource ownership and cleanup
docs.text:
The application creates the engine and remains responsible for its lifecycle, including engine.dispose() when the application no longer needs it.

  • SqlSource obtains a connection for the query and closes the result and connection when reading completes or raises.
  • SqlSink opens a transaction for each non-empty batch using SQLAlchemy's transaction context. The context commits on success and rolls back the current batch on an exception.
  • ETLRelay does not close or dispose the engine passed to either component.

A typical application can share one engine between a source and a sink, including components in one pipeline, then dispose it once the pipeline and any verification queries are complete.

SqlSource explicitly closes its SQLAlchemy result after row retrieval, including when result validation or iteration fails. Its connection is released on successful completion and failure.

SqlSink releases its per-batch transaction resources when the transaction context exits.

Neither component disposes a caller-supplied Engine.

A configured pipeline instead uses the shared SQL engine factory. PipelineBuilder.close() is responsible for releasing the engines owned by that factory after the pipeline has finished.

docs.title: Database support
docs.text:
The API accepts a SQLAlchemy Engine, so the actual connection URL, dialect, and DBAPI driver determine which database can be connected to. SQLite is the reference backend used by the automated integration tests because it is self-contained and repeatable.

The project does not currently promise equal behavior or continuous integration coverage for every SQLAlchemy dialect. A database other than SQLite needs its appropriate SQLAlchemy dialect/driver and should be verified against the queries, column types, constraints, and transaction behavior used by an application. Connection URLs may contain credentials in real deployments; examples in this documentation deliberately use in-memory SQLite and contain no credentials.

docs.title: Query values and identifiers
docs.text:
SQL parameters are for values, not identifiers. Use :parameter_name markers and the parameters mapping with SqlSource:

SqlSource(
    engine,
    "SELECT id FROM orders WHERE customer_id = :customer_id",
    parameters={"customer_id": 42},
)

Do not interpolate untrusted values into SQL text. If a query needs a dynamic table name, column name, or sort order, bind parameters cannot provide it. Prefer fixed query text; otherwise construct the identifier from a trusted allowlist and use the appropriate database/dialect-aware SQLAlchemy API. SqlSource accepts caller-authored SQL text and is not a SQL parser, query-policy engine, or authorization boundary.

SqlSink receives its destination table and optional schema separately and delegates table reflection/insert statement construction to SQLAlchemy. Do not treat this as validation of an arbitrary source query or as permission to pass uncontrolled identifiers into SQL text.

docs.title: Empty-data behavior
docs.text:
Input condition SqlSource SqlSink Query returns no rows Returns no batches Not applicable Source yields no batches The pipeline does not invoke the sink An empty iterable performs no inserts Batch has zero rows but a schema Query results do not generate this shape for an empty query Skips the zero-row batch without inserting rows Non-empty result/batch Returns one result batch Inserts the batch rows if validation succeeds

An empty iterable and a zero-row batch are distinct in the core pipeline. SQL source queries with no rows produce the former; a sink may also receive an explicitly constructed zero-row batch from another source.

docs.title: Append and transaction boundaries
docs.text:
SqlSink opens a separate transaction for every non-empty batch. Each batch is atomic within its own transaction, subject to the database and driver. A successful batch is committed before the next batch's transaction is started.

Consequently, if a pipeline writes several batches and a later batch fails, earlier successfully committed batches remain in the destination. ETLRelay does not provide one transaction across an entire pipeline or a whole iterable of batches. A retry performed by an application may append rows again unless the application has separately designed an idempotency strategy; ETLRelay does not retry automatically.

A successful batch commit is reported only after the transaction context exits successfully. Errors during execution or commit propagate to the caller without a successful-commit event.

Zero-row batches are skipped before table reflection, column validation, or transaction creation. When SqlSink is called directly, an empty batch therefore does not establish or validate the destination schema.

Pipeline-level schema validation remains separate and includes zero-row batches.

A SQL sink batch is considered successfully committed only after SQLAlchemy's transaction context exits successfully.

Commit-related errors propagate to the caller. ETLRelay does not emit a successful batch-commit event for a transaction whose commit fails.

Zero-row batches are skipped before table reflection, column validation, or transaction creation.

When SqlSink is called directly, a zero-row batch therefore does not validate the destination table or establish a destination schema.

When called through Pipeline, zero-row batches still participate in the pipeline's separate output-schema compatibility checks.

docs.title: Limitations and out-of-scope behavior
docs.text:
• No replace mode: writes append rows only. There is no replace argument or table truncation behavior.
  • No table creation or schema migration: the destination table must pre-exist with a compatible schema.
  • No ORM integration: SQLAlchemy ORM models and sessions are not part of these component contracts.
  • No automatic retries: connection, query, constraint, and write failures propagate to the caller.
  • No pipeline-wide transaction: transactions are scoped to individual non-empty sink batches.
  • No database-specific bulk strategy or pagination guarantee: a non-empty source query is materialized as one batch, so large query results may require significant memory.
  • No universal dialect guarantee: SQLite is the continuously exercised integration backend; other configured SQLAlchemy dialects need application-level verification.
  • No automatic credential management or authorization layer: the caller is responsible for configuring connections, managing secrets, and limiting database permissions.

These limits are deliberate. Additional write modes, ORM support, migrations, retries, pagination, and broader database integration should be introduced only with explicit requirements and corresponding tests.

docs.title: SQL components in YAML configuration
docs.text:
ETLRelay supports SQL sources and sinks through schema-version-1 YAML configuration and through direct Python construction.

In YAML, SQL components use environment-variable references rather than literal connection URLs. PipelineBuilder resolves the configured component registrations and preflights required connection-variable references before invoking component factories.

The v0.9.0 release retains these configuration properties and documents their validation, error-reporting, and resource-lifecycle contracts.

Unlike the direct Python API, the configuration builder does not receive an Engine argument. It receives the name of an environment variable containing the SQLAlchemy connection URL. PipelineBuilder first resolves all component registrations and calls the shared SqlEngineFactory.preflight() for the referenced variable names. If a variable is missing or empty, building fails before SQL component factories, engine creation, or configured source/sink I/O.

After preflight succeeds, the SQL factory creates engines on demand and caches them by environment-variable name. A single SqlEngineFactory is shared by the catalog's SQL source and sink factories. The caller must call PipelineBuilder.close() after the configured pipeline completes to dispose of these factory-owned engines and clear the resolved URLs.

This is separate from direct Python usage: a caller that constructs SqlSource(engine, ...) or SqlSink(engine, ...) continues to own and dispose of that supplied engine. The configuration lifecycle does not change the direct API contract.

See YAML Configuration for environment-variable setup, redaction behavior, supported combinations, and complete runnable examples.

docs.text:
The supported convenience imports are the responsibility-level packages:

Package Public names etlrelay.core Batch, Source, Processor, Sink, TabularReader, TabularWriter, KeyValueReader, WriterError etlrelay.pipeline Pipeline etlrelay.processors SelectColumns, RenameColumns, FilterRows etlrelay.readers CsvReader, ParquetReader, YamlReader, YamlDocumentError etlrelay.writers CsvWriter, ParquetWriter etlrelay.sources FileSource, SqlSource etlrelay.sinks FileSink, SqlSink etlrelay.storage FileSystem, FileSystemError, LocalFileSystem etlrelay.security PathValidator, PathValidationError

The root etlrelay package does not provide an umbrella re-export API. Configuration services and registries use the documented implementation-module imports, as shown by the generated API reference.

The old Reader and Writer class names are removed without aliases. Their modules remain etlrelay.core.reader and etlrelay.core.writer to avoid an additional import-path break. KeyValueReader remains in the reader module. This explicitly revises the earlier module-renaming plan and corrects the changelog's inaccurate claim that those modules were removed.

ReaderError remains importable from etlrelay.core.reader; it is not a promise that every reader normalizes failures to that exception. WriterError is used by the Parquet writer for empty iterables and incompatible schemas.

Protocols use structural typing. Runtime isinstance checks on protocols only check member availability; they do not prove return types, stream ownership, or behavioral substitutability. Both reader protocols contain read, so they must not be distinguished solely through runtime protocol checks.

docs.title: Contract details retained for v1.0
docs.text:
• Type annotations define expected Python inputs. This review does not add blanket runtime type validation or widen constructor signatures.
  • Batch can contain duplicate Arrow field names. Selection requires requested names to be unambiguous, filtering requires its target to be unambiguous, renaming requires unique final names, and SQL boundaries reject duplicates.
  • Processors preserve the relevant field types and nullability. FilterRows uses Arrow comparisons without custom casting and excludes false/null results. YAML filter values remain restricted to strings, integers, floats, and booleans; SQL bound parameters additionally accept null. Direct Python values follow Arrow's comparison support and are not constrained by the YAML schema.
  • Output schema enforcement belongs to Pipeline; direct writers and sinks retain their own format/database checks. There is no implicit reconciliation.
  • Tabular readers/writers borrow streams. Callers keep streams open while consuming lazy input. File components own and close streams they open.
  • An entirely empty pipeline source leaves its sink untouched. Direct calls to a file sink still open/truncate its destination, even with no batches.
  • CSV writing of no batches writes no bytes. Parquet writing requires at least one batch to establish its schema. A zero-row batch with a schema is valid.
  • SQL result/connection lifetimes end before Arrow conversion. Sources materialize all result rows, so batch-oriented execution does not guarantee bounded memory.
  • Direct SQL components borrow caller-owned engines. Configuration-built engines belong to the shared engine factory and are released through builder cleanup.
  • File writes are not atomic. SQL batch transactions do not provide pipeline-wide rollback or automatic retry/idempotency.
  • validate reads the configuration file and checks document/schema rules. run additionally resolves component registrations, preflights SQL environment references, builds components, executes, and closes builder resources.
  • CLI exit codes remain 0 success, 1 unexpected internal error, 2 usage error, 3 configuration/build failure, and 4 execution/cleanup failure.
  • Library errors may include native third-party details. CLI execution diagnostics omit underlying messages; controlled logs do not establish universal redaction.

docs.title: Exception boundary correction
docs.text:
YamlDocumentError subclasses ValueError, preserving existing library catches for YAML root-shape errors. Syntax, duplicate-key, and multiple-document errors remain yaml.YAMLError. ConfigLoader continues to propagate reader errors.

The CLI catches the specific document error and emits a controlled shape message. It does not classify every ValueError as user configuration failure; unrelated internal errors retain exit code 1.

docs.title: Defect found and corrected
docs.text:
Previously, the native Parquet writer's context-manager exit could replace an upstream processing error with an error writing the footer. A regression test reproduced this against a real PyArrow writer and a deterministic failing stream.

ParquetWriter now explicitly attempts finalization after failure, retains the original exception, and logs a secondary finalization error using its type only. A finalization error after otherwise successful serialization still propagates. There is no public signature, configuration-schema, or CLI exit-code change.

This does not make file output atomic. A failed footer may leave unreadable output. Successfully finalized earlier batches may remain readable after an upstream failure; they are still partial results from a failed run.

docs.title: Test design and limits
docs.text:
• Permission failures use patched file opening rather than chmod assumptions; behavior stays deterministic under privileged users and across platforms.
  • Connection refusal uses SQLAlchemy engine doubles rather than external services. Actual SQLite syntax and transaction failures use local databases.
  • The processor/output test uses a two-batch reader double and real CSV/Parquet serialization, retaining stream references so garbage collection cannot hide missing cleanup.
  • Normal-path stream, SQL result/connection, and engine cleanup tests remain in place. New assertions supplement those existing tests rather than duplicating a complete source/sink combination matrix.
  • Redaction evidence concerns ETLRelay-controlled diagnostics. Native library exceptions can contain sensitive data; arbitrary third-party exceptions, application handlers, filenames, and configuration keys are not universally sanitized. Test sentinels do not establish universal sanitization.
  • Resource release means closure/disposal is attempted at the owning boundary. A failing underlying close/dispose operation cannot be guaranteed to release an external resource. The tested contracts establish exception precedence and continued cleanup attempts where documented.

The Parquet precedence defect is addressed in this change. No other unresolved release-blocking defect was identified by this audit. Required CI and integration into dev remain prerequisites for closing the ticket. Supported-platform installation verification remains assigned to 0.9.0-06.

docs.title: Migration to v0.9.0
docs.text: This page describes changes from v0.8.0 to v0.9.0. Install etlrelay==0.9.0 before updating and testing the Python imports below.

docs.title: Rename the tabular protocols
docs.text:
Update imports and type annotations:

Before After from etlrelay.core import Reader from etlrelay.core import TabularReader from etlrelay.core import Writer from etlrelay.core import TabularWriter from etlrelay.core.reader import Reader from etlrelay.core.reader import TabularReader from etlrelay.core.writer import Writer from etlrelay.core.writer import TabularWriter

There are no legacy class aliases. Module paths remain core.reader and core.writer. Concrete CsvReader, ParquetReader, CsvWriter, and ParquetWriter names and constructor signatures are unchanged.

The contracts remain:

from collections.abc import Iterable
from typing import BinaryIO

from etlrelay.core import Batch, TabularReader, TabularWriter


def copy_batches(reader: TabularReader, writer: TabularWriter,
                 source: BinaryIO, destination: BinaryIO) -> None:
    batches: Iterable[Batch] = reader.read(source)
    writer.write(batches, destination)

Both streams are borrowed and must remain open while batches are consumed. The caller closes them. File sources/sinks own streams they open themselves.

KeyValueReader remains the separate mapping-document protocol, returning one Mapping[str, Any]. It is used by ConfigLoader; it does not produce tabular batches or row-record sequences. KeyValueWriter and generic record conversion remain deferred. No replacement configuration reader is required.

docs.title: Account for corrected failures
docs.text:
• Invalid YAML root shapes now raise YamlDocumentError, a ValueError subclass. Existing except ValueError handlers continue to work. It is available from etlrelay.readers and etlrelay.readers.yaml.
  • CLI run and validate classify these document errors as configuration failures with exit code 3, rather than unexpected-error code 1.
  • SelectColumns raises ValueError for ambiguous requested field names, replacing the underlying Arrow KeyError previously exposed in that case.
  • RenameColumns rejects duplicate final names even when duplicate fields originated in the input batch. Correct the input names or selection first.
  • If upstream processing/serialization and Parquet finalization both fail, the original error is preserved. Secondary finalization failures are logged by type without their messages. Finalization-only failures still propagate.

File output can still be partial or unreadable after a failed run. SQL output still commits per nonempty batch; rerunning may append duplicates. These fixes add no atomic replacement, retries, or pipeline-wide rollback.

docs.title: Dependencies and configuration
docs.text:
Polars is no longer a runtime dependency because the frozen implementation uses PyArrow. Applications using Polars independently must declare it themselves.

YAML schema version 1, supported component names, CLI commands, and the remaining exit codes are unchanged. validate parses and checks the schema; SQL environment resolution occurs during run construction. No YAML migration or new storage integration is required.

Use the API reference, failure matrix, and packaging record for detailed contracts and verification evidence.

  • Complete dependency-requirement comparison for both archive metadata sets, including bounds, extras, and environment markers; regression tests reject missing dependencies, changed/missing bounds, and extra dependencies.
  • Required Apache licence and notice files in both archive types.
  • Public component imports and direct CSV-to-Parquet-to-SQLite pipelines, including SQL source readback with data/schema assertions.
  • The existing installed CLI version/help, YAML validation, and CSV execution checks for each artifact.
  • Both-artifact smoke checks in the quality job, all compatibility jobs, and the existing TestPyPI/PyPI verification workflows.

There is no new support-matrix combination or runtime feature. Existing CI job names are retained; the compatibility steps now test both archive types.

docs.title: Runtime dependencies and metadata
docs.text:
Runtime imports require PyArrow, PyYAML, SQLAlchemy, and Typer. Their existing version constraints remain unchanged. Standard-library SQLite supplies the reference database driver; other drivers are not bundled or claimed as tested.

Polars had no imports in the runtime implementation and no frozen-feature use case. It is removed from runtime metadata and the lockfile. packaging is an explicit CI-tool dependency for standards-aware requirement comparison, not a new runtime dependency. Remaining locked package versions are unchanged.

At the packaging-review baseline, metadata declared 0.8.0 and CPython >=3.12,<3.15; those verification archives did not replace the published files. Beta preparation sets version 0.9.0 without changing the supported Python range. See the final readiness record for release-build results and integrated CI requirements.

The archive checker verifies the 64 source Python modules, distribution name, version, Python requirement, runtime requirements, licence/notice inclusion, and the etlrelay = etlrelay.cli:main wheel entry point. Installation from the sdist independently exercises its build metadata and generated entry point.

Checks validate selected resolved dependency versions within the declared ranges; they do not test every possible dependency-version combination.

docs.text:
Ticket: 0.9.0-04 — Complete representative pipeline coverage. Baseline: dev commit 3f88414.

The frozen scope includes local CSV, local Parquet, and SQLAlchemy/SQLite. S3 and other remote storage are deferred and are not required by this matrix. Other SQLAlchemy dialects are not verified by these tests.

docs.text:
The existing parametrized integration test tests/integration/test_configured_pipeline_combinations.py::test_supported_source_sink_combination_runs_end_to_end loads real YAML, validates it with the default catalog, builds a pipeline, executes it, and checks persisted data for all nine pairs below. Each pair uses processors: []; the bracketed text is its pytest parameter ID.

Source Sink Existing YAML case Representative processed coverage CSV CSV [csv-csv] Direct Python, YAML/Python equivalence, and installed CLI CSV Parquet [csv-parquet] No additional processed case needed for this format boundary CSV SQLite [csv-sql] Direct Python mixed-I/O pipeline Parquet CSV [parquet-csv] No additional processed case needed for this format boundary Parquet Parquet [parquet-parquet] Direct Python processor chain Parquet SQLite [parquet-sql] New installed CLI processor chain SQLite CSV [sql-csv] Direct Python mixed-I/O pipeline SQLite Parquet [sql-parquet] New installed CLI processor chain SQLite SQLite [sql-sql] Direct Python parameterized query and filter

It builds one wheel, installs it with locked runtime dependencies in an isolated environment, verifies import isolation, and runs subprocesses from temporary working directories. No additional installation fixture or test framework is introduced.

The two new CLI cases verify that validate leaves the destination unchanged before run. They reuse the existing YAML-writing, file-configuration, and subprocess helpers. SQLite databases and Parquet files are temporary; no external database service or credentials are required.

docs.title: Schema interpretation
docs.text:
CSV and SQL outputs are checked against their expected inferred types for the chosen records. These assertions do not promise preservation of arbitrary source schemas through CSV serialization or SQL value inference.

The direct Parquet pipeline explicitly starts with an int32 field and both nullable and nonnullable fields. Its output must preserve those field contracts through select, rename, filter, and serialization. A null predicate input is excluded; the installed CLI cases separately preserve a null in a retained output field.
